• Deterministic environment selection from either the compatibility root baseharbor.yaml or one complete envs/<environment>/baseharbor.yaml.
  • Environment-scoped protected state under .baseharbor/environments/<environment>/ for multi-environment deployments.
  • Typed policy results using allow, warn and deny.
  • baha policy check [-e ENV] [-o json].
  • baha policy explain [-e ENV] [-o json].
  • Read-only MCP tools:
  • baseharbor.policy.check
  • baseharbor.policy.explain

docs.title: Changed
docs.text:
• Repository root, selected manifest and deployment state are separate concepts.
  • Environment manifests are complete application intents; BaseHarbor does not merge hidden overlays.
  • Repository workload discovery continues from the actual Git/application root even when the selected manifest is below envs/.
  • Repository-aware lifecycle/read operations use the common environment resolver.
  • Backup, restore, update and destroy stay bound to the selected environment.
  • Existing Compose workload-security findings are represented through the shared policy result model.

docs.title: Security
docs.text:
• Policy remains deny-by-default and fail-closed.
  • BASEHARBOR_WORKLOAD_SECURITY_MODE=development cannot weaken a managed/test/production/custom environment.
  • The only current workload-security override is the explicit development-only host-device acknowledgement; privileged/runtime-socket/host-namespace/critical-host-mount/dangerous-capability findings remain non-overridable.
  • Environment-specific state isolates deployment inputs, normalized TLS material, generated runtime state and application state.

docs.title: Compatibility & upgrade notes
docs.text:
• Existing single-environment repositories keep their current .baseharbor state layout.
  • A root baseharbor.yaml remains valid.
  • Selecting a different environment with -e/--environment, or selecting an envs/<environment>/baseharbor.yaml, uses an isolated environment state root.
  • Multiple environment manifests without an explicit selection fail closed.
  • Manifest v1 remains the portable application compatibility surface.
  • Kubernetes/OpenShift runtime behavior is unchanged and remains future work.

docs.title: BaseHarbor v0.4.14
docs.text:
v0.4.14 completes the shared reconciliation, security and lifecycle semantics required before the v0.5 compatibility freeze.

The release does not implement Kubernetes or OpenShift. It defines runtime-neutral reconciliation behavior that current Compose providers and future runtime/delivery adapters can reuse.

docs.title: Added
docs.text:
• Shared internal/reconciliation domain model with typed Desired, Observed, Diff and Ownership state.
  • Typed reconciliation states:
  • missing
  • in_sync
  • drift
  • conflict
  • foreign_ownership
  • unsupported
  • degraded
  • Typed actions:
  • create
  • noop
  • repair
  • destroy
  • observe
  • blocked
  • Optional provider-native observation through the existing capability lifecycle.
  • Provider conformance checks for typed reconciliation and verified convergence.

docs.title: Lifecycle semantics
docs.text:
The shared lifecycle now follows:

intent
  -> resolve
  -> preflight
  -> observe
  -> diff + ownership decision
  -> mutation only when required
  -> bind
  -> verify
  -> observe again
  -> verified convergence

Existing providers remain compatible. Providers that implement the reconciliation observation interface gain typed state and core-level mutation decisions without introducing a second lifecycle engine.

docs.title: Security and ownership
docs.text:
• Conflict, unsupported, degraded and foreign-ownership states fail closed before provider mutation.
  • A BaseHarbor-owned missing resource resolves to create.
  • A BaseHarbor-owned stable resource resolves to a core-level noop; provider mutation is skipped.
  • BaseHarbor-owned drift resolves to repair.
  • External ownership is observe-only.
  • Post-verification observation prevents a lifecycle from reporting success when BaseHarbor-owned state did not actually converge.
  • Ownership-safe destroy remains a core requirement; BaseHarbor must never delete foreign resources.

docs.title: Compatibility
docs.text:
• Manifest v1 is unchanged.
  • Provider Integration Contract v1 remains the provider boundary.
  • Existing providers that do not yet expose typed observation retain their previous lifecycle behavior.
  • No Kubernetes/OpenShift fields are added to portable application intent.
  • No Argo CD, Flux or other product-specific delivery mechanism becomes part of the application contract.

docs.title: BaseHarbor v0.4.15.1
docs.text:
BaseHarbor v0.4.15.1 is a focused hotfix release for defects found during real repository adoption and post-v0.4.15 lifecycle testing.

It preserves the v0.4.15 application contract while correcting the operator-visible runtime project model before productive installations exist.

docs.title: Runtime Broker compatibility
docs.text:
A CLI rebuilt from the released source line could previously reject the matching v0.4.15 Runtime Broker solely because the Git commit SHA differed.

v0.4.15.1 keeps Git SHA as provenance but treats the versioned runtime contract as the compatibility boundary. Deterministic version mismatches now fail immediately instead of waiting through the readiness retry window.

docs.title: Repository adoption and Compose behavior
docs.text:
Real-world Compose repositories exposed several adoption gaps.

v0.4.15.1:

  • resolves YAML anchors and merge keys during repository inspection;
  • fails explicitly on unsupported Compose include or extends inheritance instead of silently losing services;
  • refuses deterministic init when repository ambiguity has not been resolved by explicit intent;
  • detects database bootstrap mounts such as docker-entrypoint-initdb.d and stops before replacing a database if the bootstrap would otherwise be discarded;
  • automatically remaps occupied fixed host-port bindings through a BaseHarbor-owned deployment override without rewriting the repository;
  • prevents interactive TTY stdin from leaking into Compose/BuildKit progress commands and causing indefinite rebuild hangs.

docs.title: Lifecycle and registry correctness
docs.text:
Application and installation state is more consistent after partial failures and stop/destroy operations.

  • baha app down records the observed stopped state.
  • baha app list tolerates incomplete deployment directories and reports warnings instead of failing the complete list.
  • Global baha status shows BaseHarbor-native target, control-plane and application information rather than raw Compose output.
  • Out-of-repository restore verifies that the source repository can be resolved before durable state is changed.
  • baha destroy --all removes BaseHarbor-owned Runtime Broker volumes while still preserving application-owned workload data.

docs.title: Targets
docs.text:
The implicit local target now appears in baha target list.

Creating a new target no longer silently makes it the default unless --default is supplied, and invalid target names now explain the accepted lowercase slug rules.

docs.title: MCP lifecycle
docs.text:
Mutating MCP operations can legitimately exceed common client request timeouts during image pulls, builds and readiness convergence.

Once a mutating lifecycle request has been accepted, BaseHarbor now keeps its convergence independent from client-request cancellation so a short client timeout does not intentionally truncate the deployment half-way through. Detached convergence is still bounded by a BaseHarbor-owned 30-minute lifecycle deadline.

Clients should still use a realistic lifecycle timeout; 300 seconds is the recommended general-purpose starting point. Read-only MCP tools may be auto-allowed while mutating tools remain approval-gated.

docs.title: Initialization and Target configuration
docs.text:
The top-level baha init command no longer creates the obsolete global deployment: single-node configuration.

baseharbor.yaml remains the portable repository application contract. Use baha app init for application intent and baha target create for deployment destination/runtime selection. Keeping these concerns separate avoids mixing local control-plane topology into portable application configuration.

docs.title: Shared OpenBao restart recovery
docs.text:
OpenBao recovery handling now belongs to the effective Target/shared-provider lifecycle rather than to an individual application.

After successful bootstrap, BaseHarbor persists only the absolute recovery-file path under target.openbao.recovery-file; the recovery material itself remains operator-held outside normal BaseHarbor runtime/application state. On later restarts, baha up can automatically unseal the shared OpenBao provider when that referenced file is present. An explicit --recovery-file PATH remains authoritative, while a broken persisted reference fails closed with actionable guidance.

The implicit local Target is materialized only when persistent Target state is actually required.

docs.title: Docker Runtime Broker logging
docs.text:
A Docker-only observability regression could leave Runtime Broker stdout visible through docker logs while its provider stream never reached Alloy/Loki.

v0.4.15.1 restores the stable Runtime Broker Compose service identity broker, which restores reliable Docker syslog forwarding while retaining the consolidated application stack and all current runtime URLs/contracts.

docs.title: Compatibility
docs.text:
Manifest v1 remains unchanged.

Docker remains Compose-based and Podman remains native Quadlet/systemd-user based. The fixed-port fallback is implemented as a deployment-local override with aligned semantics across both providers.

Operator-visible Compose identity now follows provider scope: target-wide shared components are grouped under bh-<target>-shared, while application runtime/workload and application-scoped providers use bh-<target>-<application>-<environment>. External providers remain outside BaseHarbor-owned projects. Provider state, ownership and physical resource identities remain typed and independently managed.

docs.title: Security
docs.text: The shared OpenBao recovery-file change persists only a filesystem path reference. Recovery keys remain outside BaseHarbor-managed application/runtime state, existing recovery files are never overwritten during bootstrap, and an explicitly persisted but unavailable recovery reference fails closed instead of silently selecting different material.

docs.title: Intentionally deferred work
docs.text:
Stable opaque application, deployment and provider-instance identities remain planned for v0.4.19. v0.4.15.1 already preserves the required ownership boundary: shared OpenBao is Target/provider-owned and application scopes do not own the shared provider instance.

The broader Docker/Podman log-collection convergence tracked separately is also deferred; this hotfix only restores the proven stable Docker Runtime Broker service identity.

For the complete technical list, see the v0.4.15.1 changelog.

docs.title: BaseHarbor v0.4.15
docs.text: BaseHarbor v0.4.15 is a major step toward the v0.5 contract freeze. It expands BaseHarbor from a strong local developer platform into a more complete, agent-native and runtime-neutral application lifecycle while keeping portable application intent independent from concrete infrastructure products.

docs.title: Full MCP lifecycle
docs.text:
The MCP/JSON interface is no longer limited to inspection.

Agents can now use the supported BaseHarbor lifecycle through the same semantic core as the CLI, including:

inspect -> plan -> apply -> status -> doctor -> observe -> update -> repair -> backup -> restore -> destroy

Policy, ownership, reconciliation, verification and approval requirements remain enforced regardless of whether BaseHarbor is operated by a human or an agent.

No generic shell, Docker, Compose or Podman execution interface is exposed.

docs.title: Native Podman with Quadlets
docs.text:
Docker continues to use Docker Compose.

Podman now uses native rootless Quadlets managed through systemd --user instead of relying on podman-compose.

The same BaseHarbor application and provider semantics are preserved across both runtimes, while Podman now follows its native runtime model more closely.

docs.title: Secure service access
docs.text:
Managed service access now follows a common TLS and authentication model across environments.

BaseHarbor supports managed local PKI as well as external/BYOC PKI while keeping trust, credentials and transport details out of portable application intent.

Applications continue to consume standard URLs, environment variables and file bindings while BaseHarbor manages the deployment-side security model.

docs.title: Complete metrics, logs and traces
docs.text:
The observability model has been completed across:

  • metrics;
  • logs;
  • traces.

Application workloads, managed providers, Runtime Broker and Runtime Executor now participate in the same provider-neutral observability model.

Prometheus, Loki, Tempo and OpenTelemetry remain reference implementations behind portable contracts rather than becoming part of the application API.

docs.title: CLI Targets and installation-wide lifecycle
docs.text:
v0.4.15 introduces first-class Targets as a new deployment dimension.

A deployment is now identified by:

target + application + environment

This allows the same application and environment to exist independently across different Docker or Podman Targets while BaseHarbor keeps runtime state, providers, networks, volumes and ownership state isolated.

Targets are available consistently through the CLI, shell integration, JSON and MCP interfaces and establish the runtime boundary needed for future Kubernetes and OpenShift support.

The Target model also enables installation-wide cleanup across all known Targets:

baha destroy --all

Cleanup remains ownership-safe: application source repositories and foreign or external application-owned resources are preserved.

docs.title: Smarter init and repository adoption
docs.text:
BaseHarbor is better at understanding existing repositories before asking the developer to describe them manually.

Repository inspection can distinguish application workloads from replaceable infrastructure, detect supported capabilities and guide adoption without silently inventing intent when a repository is ambiguous.

Guided init now includes clearer capability selection, improved secret handling, deterministic workload selection and more actionable failures.

The application model also became more provider-neutral during this work: generic service families such as sql and cache are used instead of product-specific application intent, while standards-based service bindings remain the integration surface for workloads.

docs.title: Compatibility
docs.text:
Manifest v1 remains the compatibility contract.

Docker remains Compose-based. Supported Podman execution now uses native Quadlets.

Kubernetes and OpenShift Targets fit the new Target architecture, but runtime execution for them is intentionally deferred to a later release.

For the complete technical change list, compatibility details and security notes, see the v0.4.15 changelog.

docs.title: BaseHarbor v0.4.16
docs.text: BaseHarbor v0.4.16 completes the recovery and audit/evidence track planned for the final v0.4 productization line.

docs.title: Selectable application recovery units
docs.text:
Backup is now modeled as one typed application recovery unit instead of a fixed SQL-and-secrets snapshot.

Supported application-owned recovery state includes:

  • application metadata;
  • managed SQL data;
  • the application-owned OpenBao secret scope;
  • managed S3 object contents;
  • BaseHarbor-owned repository workload named volumes;
  • selectable application log history;
  • application/runtime identity reconstruction.

Interactive backup and automation use the same state classes. Guided backup lets an operator choose supported recovery classes, while scripts use --include-state and --exclude-state.

Restore validates the complete recovery manifest and selected payloads before destructive mutation. Success is reported only after restored state, runtime identities, workload readiness and Doctor verification pass.

External named volumes, bind mounts and external data stores remain outside BaseHarbor ownership and are represented explicitly rather than silently copied.

Metrics and trace history are intentionally still unsupported recovery contributors because BaseHarbor does not yet provide a safe application-scoped restore path for those histories.

docs.title: Audit and evidence v1
docs.text:
v0.4.16 adds a shared evidence model built from the same plan, policy, status, doctor, recovery and lifecycle semantics already used by BaseHarbor.

Human operators can inspect it with:

baha app evidence

Automation can export the deterministic machine representation with:

baha app evidence -o json

Agents receive the same typed result through the read-only MCP operation:

baseharbor.evidence

The bundle separates desired state, enforced policy, observed state, verified results, explicit exceptions, unsupported controls, recovery evidence and bounded lifecycle audit history.

Meaningful completed lifecycle operations record secret-safe Target-local audit events. The export is deterministically ordered and includes a SHA-256 digest as tamper evidence.

The digest is not a digital signature, remote attestation or compliance certification.

docs.title: Real-world acceptance hardening
docs.text:
The final v0.4.16 candidate also includes fixes found while adopting public Compose applications rather than only the BaseHarbor demo:

  • deterministic init refuses to silently omit an existing repository workload;
  • effective Compose configuration changes, including interpolated .env values, participate in convergence and READY state;
  • managed SQL/cache connectivity is projected through Service Binding 1.1 with workload-native endpoints and verified TLS trust;
  • secondary database/cache aliases that still point at a replaced repository service are safely rewired when unambiguous and fail closed otherwise;
  • failed convergence remains addressable through persisted deployment lifecycle state, while older incomplete deployments can be recovered by name;
  • destroy reclaims only ownership-proven volumes that belonged exclusively to replaced repository database/cache services and preserves shared, external or unknown workload data.

The fixed Compose host-port fallback introduced in v0.4.15.1 remains covered by the v0.4.16 regression suite: occupied fixed HOST:CONTAINER bindings continue to use a deployment-local override without modifying repository source.

docs.title: Security and ownership
docs.text:
Recovery and evidence preserve the existing BaseHarbor ownership model.

  • External volumes, bind mounts and operator-owned data are never silently adopted into BaseHarbor recovery ownership.
  • Application/runtime leaf identities are reconstructed; Target-wide OpenBao PKI private keys are not copied into an application archive.
  • Audit history is bounded and owner-only.
  • Evidence excludes secret values, tokens, access keys, private keys, credential-bearing URLs, prompts and agent/model reasoning.
  • CLI and MCP use the same semantic collectors and do not expose provider-native or generic shell execution.

docs.title: Compatibility
docs.text:
Manifest v1 remains unchanged.

Existing recovery archives remain readable through the legacy recovery-manifest fallback. New v0.4.16 archives carry the typed recovery manifest and contributor semantics.

Docker Compose and Podman/Quadlet use the same logical recovery contract. Recovery discovery accepts both normalized Compose volume objects and short-syntax mounts, while physical runtime resource names remain deployment detail and are not portable application identity.

No SIEM- or compliance-vendor-specific integration is introduced; JSON output is the generic evidence export boundary.

For the complete technical list, see the v0.4.16 changelog and release audit.

docs.title: BaseHarbor v0.4.17
docs.text:
BaseHarbor v0.4.17 adds standards-first managed application identity and the minimum operator-authentication boundary required before the v0.5 contract freeze.

The release keeps the normal developer path small: local dev remains trusted-local, while test and prod require an authenticated operator. Applications consume standard OIDC/OAuth2 interfaces rather than a BaseHarbor authentication SDK.

docs.title: Managed application identity
docs.text:
Applications can declare provider-neutral managed identity. BaseHarbor resolves the provider, creates or reconciles the application/environment identity scope, materializes a standard OIDC binding and verifies the realized state.

The managed Keycloak reference provider supports:

  • isolated application/environment realms and clients;
  • OIDC discovery and JWKS;
  • exposure-derived redirect and logout URIs;
  • scopes and claims;
  • portable MFA, TOTP, WebAuthn, passkey and passwordless requirements;
  • automatic TLS/trust;
  • ownership-aware observe, reconcile, verify and destroy.

External OIDC remains supported without requiring provider-side provisioning. Provider-native names and administration APIs do not become portable application intent.

Shared provider infrastructure does not imply shared application identities.

docs.title: Operator authentication by environment
docs.text:
Operator access is scoped to the effective Target and Environment: dev uses trusted-local mode; test and prod require authenticated OIDC operator access.

For protected environments the CLI uses standards-compliant OIDC Authorization Code + PKCE and stores only a short-lived owner-only local session.

Commands: baha login -e test, baha whoami -e test, and baha logout -e test.

The first interactive use of an unconfigured protected Target/Environment can bootstrap either the managed Keycloak operator boundary or an external OIDC provider. The resulting configuration is Target/Environment-scoped and is reused by applications on that boundary.

Application identity and BaseHarbor operator identity remain logically separate even when one physical IdP provides both.

Advanced RBAC, JIT elevation, approvals and break-glass governance remain outside v0.4.17.

docs.title: First-class shared provider lifecycle
docs.text:
v0.4.17 makes resource-efficient shared placement a core provider rule instead of a product-specific exception.

The bundled PostgreSQL and Valkey providers now support both shared and application placement. Their default is environment-bounded shared placement:

  • PostgreSQL runs once per Target/environment sharing boundary and creates application-isolated databases and least-privilege roles.
  • Valkey uses one Target-owned provider lifecycle and creates isolated per-application cache services/credentials so normal Redis/Valkey clients remain compatible without exposing sibling keys.
  • Service Binding 1.1 projections remain application-scoped even when provider infrastructure is shared.
  • Application destroy removes only the application's database/role/cache resources and bindings.
  • The shared provider survives while sibling applications still use it and is removed at the provider/Target ownership boundary.
  • Dedicated application placement remains supported for cases that require a separate provider instance.

This means ten applications requesting SQL no longer imply ten PostgreSQL provider instances by default. Shared infrastructure saves memory, CPU, image/runtime overhead and startup time without weakening application ownership.

The official v0.4.17 demo uses shared placement for every managed provider and keeps only the application workload application-scoped.

For PostgreSQL, shared lifecycle has a strict administration boundary: one internal baseharbor_admin identity is used only by BaseHarbor for provider lifecycle, while every Application + Environment + SQL instance receives its own deterministic role, own database and protected credential reference. The administrator is never emitted to application bindings. Reconcile revokes public database/schema access, verifies the application credential against its own database and checks sibling databases are denied.

Application backup/restore remains database-specific even on the shared provider. Destroy verifies protected registration plus live database ownership before terminating connections and dropping only the selected application's database/role. The Target owns the shared provider independently of application consumers. Destroying the final application removes its database/role/cache resources and credentials but leaves the provider state/runtime intact; explicit provider/Target destruction owns provider teardown.

docs.title: Provider interfaces and optional management UIs
docs.text:
The guided application flow treats provider interfaces by semantic purpose instead of product name.

Optional management surfaces currently include:

  • PostgreSQL administration through pgAdmin;
  • cache administration through Redis Commander;
  • shared object-storage administration through SeaweedFS Admin;
  • the existing shared OpenBao web UI;
  • managed identity login/account and separate Keycloak administration surfaces.

Selected development UIs are materialized automatically with managed TLS/trust and canonical HTTPS URLs. The effective Target owns one development domain, defaulting to baha.localhost, and one local HTTPS gateway. Internal random loopback ports remain runtime implementation detail and are no longer the normal developer-facing address. Docker binds the canonical development gateway to 443; rootless Podman uses deterministic port 8443 so the same hostname model works without privileged-port host configuration.

Canonical naming is deliberately short:

<app>.baha.localhost        application workload/API
pgadmin.baha.localhost      shared PostgreSQL UI
cache.baha.localhost        shared cache UI
storage.baha.localhost      shared object-storage UI
auth.baha.localhost         shared OIDC/login surface
auth-admin.baha.localhost   shared identity administration
secrets.baha.localhost      shared OpenBao UI
metrics.baha.localhost      shared Prometheus UI

Application-scoped provider surfaces, when explicitly selected, use <app>-<service>.<dev-domain>. External providers retain provider-owned URLs.

A shared provider creates one administration surface for the provider boundary rather than one UI per application. Test/prod administrative surfaces remain restricted/non-public by default.

The same canonical routing model applies to the normal application endpoint. An unambiguous development workload receives https://<app>.<dev-domain> automatically and Swagger/OpenAPI is exposed beneath the same host at /swagger/. status, doctor and structured status output report canonical browser URLs rather than random loopback ports.

Managed OIDC is placement-aware. With the default shared Keycloak provider, the issuer uses https://auth.<dev-domain>; an explicitly application-scoped identity provider uses an application-qualified host. Development workloads receive that same canonical issuer and the development-gateway trust binding, while provider-internal administration/readiness endpoints remain private implementation detail.

docs.title: Unified development access
docs.text:
Development Targets also own one BaseHarbor-managed management login. The default username is developer; BaseHarbor generates a strong password and exposes it only through the explicit baha dev credentials command.

When managed Identity is present, BaseHarbor reconciles the same developer identity through managed OIDC. Provider surfaces that require native authentication reuse the same development credential through provider-specific adapters. Service credentials such as database passwords, S3 keys and runtime identities remain separate least-privilege credentials.

The development domain can be inspected or changed with baha dev domain [DOMAIN]. The wizard asks for the development domain and management access once for the Target instead of asking for hostnames or separate administrator credentials per capability.

This shared local convenience credential is never used for test/prod. Protected environments continue to use individual operator OIDC sessions, policy and stronger authentication.

docs.title: Identity readiness, audit and recovery
docs.text:
status, doctor, JSON and evidence re-check the realized identity boundary instead of treating successful provisioning as permanent truth. Managed Keycloak verification covers issuer/discovery, owned realm/client state, redirect/logout drift, binding state and required authentication policy. External OIDC verification covers discovery and the materialized application binding.

Authenticated lifecycle audit events carry secret-safe operator identity and assurance context where available. Tokens, passwords, provider-admin credentials and authentication secrets are excluded.

Recovery treats portable identity intent separately from provider-held identity-directory data. The portable OIDC/client policy is reconstructed from application metadata. Provider-held users, credentials, MFA and passkey state are not claimed as recoverable without a scoped provider export; managed identity therefore remains an explicit durable recovery boundary, while external OIDC remains external.

docs.title: Environment-isolated provider registry
docs.text:
Provider registry bindings are deployment-scoped by Application plus Environment.

This fixes a pre-freeze ownership defect where two environments of the same application on one Target could otherwise replace each other's provider-registry binding even though their runtime resources were isolated.

Existing v1 registry entries without an environment remain readable and are migrated to the current deployment environment on normal reconciliation.

docs.title: Agent and read-only policy behavior
docs.text:
Read-only policy/evidence inspection no longer requires an installed Docker or Podman orchestration binary when repository Compose source can be analyzed statically.

The fallback remains fail-closed for security findings and is used only when runtime orchestration is genuinely unavailable. Runtime/provider errors are not silently converted into success.

docs.title: Development working-tree fast path
docs.text:
Local development treats the current repository working tree as valid application source. A developer can edit application code and run baha up without committing or pushing first.

When the application is already READY and the portable baseharbor.yaml contract plus protected deployment-control state are unchanged, baha up uses a workload-only fast path. The existing workload engine fingerprints build and rendered service configuration, rebuilds only affected build-backed services, recreates only configuration-changed services, waits for workload HTTP/TLS readiness, and then re-checks overall application readiness.

Changes to baseharbor.yaml, protected deployment-control state, an unavailable/unready runtime, or any condition that cannot safely prove workload-only convergence continue through the full application reconciliation path.

baha app update keeps a separate purpose: it safely advances a Git-backed application from its configured upstream and therefore continues to require a clean, non-diverged working tree. It never stashes, resets, overwrites or discards local development work.

docs.title: Final v0.4.17 release hardening
docs.text:
The final release pass tightens six release-blocking boundaries without changing Manifest v1.

  • Shared provider lifecycle: shared PostgreSQL/Valkey infrastructure is Target-owned. Application destroy never tears down the provider merely because the application was the final consumer.
  • OpenBao recovery: a stale/existing recovery output file is rejected before fresh control-plane mutation. Existing recovery material is never overwritten; --recovery-file PATH is the explicit remediation.
  • Readiness truth: RUNNING is no longer treated as READY. Compose health, HTTP/TLS probes and TCP listener probes are positive readiness signals; a running worker without such a signal is reported RUNNING/UNVERIFIED.
  • Developer gateway port: Docker prefers 443 and rootless Podman prefers 8443, but collisions select a deterministic free fallback from 18443. The selected port is Target state and every canonical URL/status/doctor path reuses it.
  • Native TLS first: OpenBao, PostgreSQL, Keycloak, SeaweedFS S3, Prometheus and OTLP use native TLS. The single Target developer gateway remains the canonical browser router. Dedicated adapters remain only where they add a real security/protocol boundary, such as cache UI TLS or the currently coordinated Loki/Tempo ingestion edge.
  • Dependency/security audit: go-oidc 3.21.0 and OpenBao 2.7.0 are adopted. OpenBao uses a dedicated least-privilege database/user in the existing PostgreSQL control-plane provider with verify-full, native TLS reload and hybrid-PQC-first TLS; no legacy storage.file or intermediate Raft compatibility path remains. Go-1.26-requiring x/crypto/x/sys updates and unrelated CI/toolchain majors remain deliberately deferred. #533 tracks the yaml.v3 replacement investigation.

Certificate rotation follows each native provider's supported reload model: Keycloak polls its certificate files, Prometheus re-reads web TLS material on requests, SeaweedFS uses a reloading certificate provider, OTLP uses a bounded TLS reload interval, and OpenBao 2.7 uses native tls_auto_reload.

docs.title: Runtime Provider boundary
docs.text:
v0.4.17 establishes the provider-neutral Runtime Provider boundary required before future Kubernetes and OpenShift work.

The contract is versioned as:

baseharbor.runtime/v1

A Runtime Provider descriptor declares provider identity and version, adopted standards, workload-source compatibility, runtime realization and supported runtime capabilities. Capability negotiation is fail-closed and product-neutral.

The package structure now enforces that boundary:

internal/runtime/contract
    provider-neutral runtime contract and model

internal/runtime/resolver
    first-party provider selection and registration

internal/providers/runtime/docker
    Docker provider implementation

internal/providers/runtime/podman
    Podman/Quadlet provider implementation

Portable Core does not import concrete Docker or Podman provider packages. Static architecture tests enforce the dependency direction and prevent provider-specific implementation files from returning to the neutral runtime package.

Compose remains a first-class workload-source standard but is no longer the identity of a Runtime Provider.

Docker realizes the current Compose workload source through Docker Compose.

Podman realizes the same portable runtime semantics through native Quadlet units and rootless systemd --user. There is no podman compose fallback.

The Runtime Provider conformance coverage exercises both reference providers through the same versioned semantic contract.

docs.title: Rootless Podman parity and release hardening
docs.text:
The final v0.4.17 validation closes the remaining Docker/Podman parity gaps discovered by the native Quadlet acceptance path:

  • managed Quadlet networks retain native .network resource references and use NetworkAlias= rather than embedding legacy alias options in the network value;
  • external workload/provider networks use the same native Quadlet alias model, restoring rootless Podman DNS for runtime-executor, metrics scraping and canonical development routing;
  • BaseHarbor preserves shared Podman networks while active sibling consumers still use them;
  • rootless candidate-image build, verification and Quadlet execution share the same Podman storage context;
  • Podman service-state observation reads published ports back from the running container so HTTP/TLS workload readiness has the same positive evidence available on Docker;
  • runtime-executor readiness diagnostics expose the failing downstream dependency, and Podman readiness budgets account for the slower native Quadlet/systemd startup path without weakening fail-closed checks.

The targeted Podman guided acceptance verifies this path end to end before the full pre-release gate.

docs.title: Runtime-neutral logs
docs.text:
Docker and Podman now converge behind one runtime-neutral log-source boundary.

BaseHarbor normalizes workload, application-provider and platform-provider log sources to the same semantic identity:

application
environment
source class
provider
service

Docker currently attaches container stdout/stderr through its syslog logging driver. Podman uses journald through the native Quadlet/systemd realization. Those transport details stay behind the runtime adapter.

Podman verification now checks the currently running project/service instead of accepting log configuration unconditionally. Invalid ownership, provider identity, signal kind or runtime target fails closed before Loki verification.

No proprietary logging protocol is introduced. Existing runtime logging, RFC5424 syslog, systemd journal semantics, Alloy and Loki remain the implementation standards.

docs.title: Standards-first runtime architecture
docs.text:
The Runtime Provider review documents the adoption/delegation boundary for:

  • OCI Image Specification;
  • OCI Distribution Specification;
  • OCI Runtime Specification;
  • Compose Specification;
  • Kubernetes API;
  • CRI;
  • CNI;
  • CSI;
  • Kubernetes Gateway API;
  • Service Binding Specification;
  • Crossplane composition/provider patterns.

BaseHarbor reuses or delegates to these standards where they already define the required boundary. BaseHarbor-specific semantics are limited to portable intent, provider negotiation, ownership, policy, lifecycle and semantic verification where the reviewed standards do not define the required application-facing behavior.

See docs/architecture/runtime-standards-audit.md, docs/architecture/runtime-log-source-contract.md and ADR 0007.

docs.title: Intentionally deferred
docs.text:
v0.4.17 does not implement:

  • Kubernetes Runtime Provider execution;
  • OpenShift Runtime Provider execution;
  • a proprietary replacement for OCI, CRI, CNI, CSI, Gateway API or Compose;
  • advanced operator RBAC, JIT elevation, approval or break-glass governance;
  • complete repository workload-source normalization remains tracked in #519; v0.4.20 covers Compose, native Quadlet and raw Kubernetes YAML, while Helm and Kustomize are intentionally deferred to later source adapters;
  • an out-of-tree runtime process/distribution protocol before a real external-provider requirement proves the necessary transport.

The normal developer path remains intentionally small:

baha app init
baha up
baha status

Provider descriptors, negotiation and implementation packages remain infrastructure details below that workflow.

docs.title: Compatibility
docs.text:
• Manifest v1 remains the portable application contract.
  • OIDC/OAuth2 and Service Binding remain the application-facing integration boundary.
  • Keycloak, pgAdmin, Redis Commander and SeaweedFS remain reference/provider implementation details.
  • Runtime Provider identity is explicitly docker or podman; Compose remains workload-source compatibility rather than provider identity.
  • Docker Compose and Podman/Quadlet retain equivalent logical application and provider ownership semantics.
  • New implicit local Target state defaults to Docker. Podman requires native Quadlet plus a usable user-systemd session and fails closed when that environment is unavailable.
  • Existing provider-registry v1 state remains readable; environment scope is additive deployment metadata.

The reference demo workload itself is HTTPS-only. Its Compose service declares io.baseharbor.workload.protocol: https; the development gateway uses the projected workload CA and the Compose service name as SNI when routing to it. Plaintext fallback is intentionally not part of the reference path.

docs.title: Release validation
docs.text:
Release-boundary validation is prepared in two layers:

  • local/Hugging Face source validation: gofmt -l ., go vet ./..., focused provider/runtime tests and go test ./...;
  • the mandatory GitHub Pre-Release gate against the exact release candidate and immutable baseharbor-demo revision.

The final GitHub Release evidence will record the exact BaseHarbor candidate SHA, the pinned demo SHA and the successful Docker/Podman pre-release run.

docs.title: BaseHarbor v0.4.18
docs.text:
BaseHarbor v0.4.18 completes the authoring and extension foundation that must exist before the v0.5 public-contract freeze.

The release adds a first-class greenfield developer path, reusable development Stack Profiles, four ecosystem-native reference Development Adapters, multi-repository workspace resolution, optional Backstage catalog emission, stronger lifecycle teardown, capability-subset acceptance, and runtime-aware host resource preflight.

Manifest v1 remains the portable application contract. Existing brownfield repositories continue to use the normal baha app init -> baha up -> READY path.

docs.title: Greenfield application creation
docs.text:
baha app new is now the first-class greenfield entry point.

It creates a normal ecosystem-native project from application capability intent and validates the generated implementation against the resulting BaseHarbor contract.

Reference stacks in this release:

  • Go;
  • Next.js;
  • Python;
  • Quarkus.

Example:

baha app new catalog-api --stack go --http --sql --cache --telemetry
cd catalog-api
baha up

Generated applications use normal ecosystem libraries and configuration. BaseHarbor does not introduce an application framework or proprietary SDK.

The same creation flow has deterministic JSON output and a semantic MCP operation. Human CLI, structured output and MCP use the same development-domain result model.

docs.title: Reusable Stack Profiles
docs.text:
Development preferences can be captured as reusable Stack Profiles without becoming portable deployment requirements.

baha stack list
baha stack show team-api
baha stack create

The guided baha stack create wizard and deterministic flags use the same profile model. Profiles can contain multiple stable development components and can compose existing profiles with explicit conflict handling.

Application requirements, development preferences, capability providers, placement, runtime and delivery remain separate concerns.

docs.title: Development Extension Contract v1
docs.text:
v0.4.18 adds versioned machine-readable contracts for:

  • common extension descriptors;
  • provider descriptors;
  • Stack Profiles;
  • Development Plans.

Development Adapters implement deterministic Detect, Plan, Bootstrap and Validate semantics. The reference adapters prove round-trip behavior from contract to implementation and back to BaseHarbor inspection/evidence.

Provider and Development Extensions share packaging/discovery/trust mechanics where appropriate, but do not share lifecycle semantics merely for code reuse.

docs.title: Multi-repository applications and workspace wizard
docs.text:
One logical application may now span:

  • one repository;
  • a monorepo with multiple components;
  • multiple already-present local repositories/worktrees;
  • a mixture of local sources and OCI images.

The portable source model is version controlled under .baseharbor/sources.yaml. Developer-local checkout paths remain XDG-local workspace metadata and never enter portable Application Intent.

baha app workspace
baha app workspace show
baha app workspace resolve

The no-subcommand form is the guided wizard. Deterministic init, map, show and resolve commands remain available for automation.

Application and Component identity are independent from the current working directory and from developer-local checkout paths. Missing worktrees fail before mutation with actionable diagnostics.

Automatic clone/fetch/checkout/sync remains deferred to the later managed-workspace lifecycle; v0.4.18 resolves only already-present local repositories/worktrees.

docs.title: External developer portals by contract
docs.text:
Backstage is supported as the first reference portal consumer without becoming a BaseHarbor dependency.

baha app new can optionally emit a minimal application-owned catalog-info.yaml:

baha app new catalog-api \
  --stack go \
  --emit-backstage \
  --backstage-owner platform-team

Portal ownership is explicit and is never inferred from BaseHarbor ownership. Backstage lifecycle metadata is not derived from BaseHarbor dev/test/prod environment.

BaseHarbor does not embed a Backstage SDK, Catalog client, template interpreter or repository-publishing credential model. Portal integrations consume stable BaseHarbor JSON/evidence contracts and normal repository metadata.

docs.title: Capability-subset acceptance
docs.text:
The reference demo now verifies a declarative capability matrix instead of assuming that a full-stack demo proves every smaller contract.

The matrix covers:

  • workload-only;
  • SQL and optional SQL management UI;
  • cache;
  • object storage;
  • secrets;
  • identity;
  • metrics;
  • logs;
  • telemetry;
  • mixed SQL/cache and developer-core profiles;
  • the full reference combination;
  • invalid cross-capability combinations that must fail before mutation.

Contract-only matrix cases remain cheap and deterministic. Runtime acceptance starts only the providers needed by the selected reduced profile; it does not build the whole provider stack for every case.

docs.title: Lifecycle and teardown hardening
docs.text:
Application stop/destroy now use observed runtime ownership rather than reconstructing successful apply-time state.

This means partially converged deployments can still be cleaned safely when a provider binding or later lifecycle step never completed.

Owned workload containers and networks are removed before deployment state is deleted, while repository/application-owned volumes are preserved according to ownership rules.

Additional v0.4.18 lifecycle hardening includes:

  • persisted workload-port fallback applied consistently;
  • repository workload startup fails fast on terminal runtime errors;
  • canonical development gateway/identity URLs preserve the effective persisted gateway port;
  • management UI readiness follows browser redirect chains rather than treating an initial redirect as failure.

docs.title: Host resource preflight
docs.text:
Before local Docker or Podman mutation, BaseHarbor now evaluates runtime-host memory headroom using Linux:

  • MemAvailable;
  • swap state;
  • memory PSI where available;
  • a delta-aware estimate of the selected application/control-plane capabilities.

The result is classified as safe, tight or unsafe.

Unsafe headroom fails before runtime mutation. Tight headroom requires explicit interactive approval or the explicit --skip-memory-preflight override.

This evidence is deliberately runtime-scoped:

  • Docker and Podman use local runtime-host evidence;
  • Kubernetes/OpenShift do not use the CLI machine's /proc values.

Future Kubernetes/OpenShift providers must implement cluster-specific resource evidence covering capacity/allocatable resources, requests/limits, quotas and scheduling constraints.

docs.title: Pre-release architecture
docs.text:
The release validation keeps every small demo gate individually runnable for diagnosis, but the release-wide runtime proof now reuses long-lived environments.

The complete runtime semantics are exercised on both reference runtimes in four parallel lanes:

  • Docker · Core Journey;
  • Docker · Operations;
  • Podman · Core Journey;
  • Podman · Operations.

Each lane builds/loads the exact candidate once and runs a sequence of already-targeted gates against the same environment where safe. This removes repeated provider/container setup without reducing Docker/Podman semantic coverage.

Targeted workflow runs are named by purpose, for example Docker · Capability Matrix, instead of internal branch/test terminology.

docs.title: Dependency and toolchain decision
docs.text:
BaseHarbor v0.4.18 intentionally remains on:

go 1.25.0
golang.org/x/crypto v0.55.0

The available x/crypto v0.56/v0.57 line requires Go 1.26. Raising the project Go floor is a platform/toolchain decision rather than a routine dependency refresh, so that update is explicitly deferred to a later release together with the matching CI/support-documentation change.

The YAML v3 dependency has moved to the maintained go.yaml.in/yaml/v3 module.

docs.title: Compatibility
docs.text:
• Manifest v1 remains supported.
  • Existing brownfield repositories remain compatible.
  • Development metadata and local workspace mappings are additive authoring-time state.
  • Local filesystem paths do not become portable application identity.
  • Generated projects use ecosystem-native dependencies and standard service bindings.
  • Docker and Podman remain the two implemented local Runtime Providers.
  • Kubernetes/OpenShift Target definitions remain future-runtime contracts; local-host memory evidence is explicitly not reused for cluster capacity decisions.

docs.title: Intentionally deferred
docs.text:
v0.4.18 does not add:

  • automatic Git clone/fetch/pull/checkout/worktree synchronization;
  • Kubernetes Runtime Provider execution;
  • OpenShift Runtime Provider execution;
  • a Backstage runtime/API dependency;
  • a BaseHarbor application framework;
  • an implicit Go 1.26 toolchain upgrade.

Those boundaries remain additive work after the v0.5 contract freeze rather than hidden requirements in the v0.4.18 application contract.

docs.title: Release validation
docs.text:
Release-boundary evidence uses:

  • local/Hugging Face formatting, vet, source/package and contract validation first;
  • targeted Docker/Podman demo gates for failures that require real runtime evidence;
  • one final GitHub Pre-Release run against the exact v0.4.18 candidate and the immutable demo revision recorded in docs/releases/v0.4.18.demo-ref.

The successful final run is the immutable release approval used by the subsequent release/publish workflow.

docs.title: BaseHarbor v0.4.19
docs.text:
BaseHarbor v0.4.19 completes the remaining service and provider foundations planned before the v0.5 contract freeze.

The release adds portable messaging, durable key-value and document-database capabilities, first-class External/BYO provider onboarding, organization-wide platform configuration, and clearer Runtime/Delivery provider boundaries.

docs.title: New portable service capabilities
docs.text:
v0.4.19 adds three provider-neutral service families:

  • database.key-value/v1
  • database.document/v1
  • messaging.queue/v1
  • messaging.pubsub/v1
  • messaging.stream/v1

The reference providers are:

  • Valkey for durable key-value data;
  • MongoDB for document databases;
  • RabbitMQ for queue, pub/sub and stream messaging.

Application intent describes the capability an application needs, not the implementation product.

A durable key-value database is now also explicitly distinct from cache.key-value: both may use Valkey, but they have different durability, lifecycle and recovery semantics.

docs.title: External and BYO providers
docs.text:
Existing enterprise infrastructure can now be registered and consumed through the normal BaseHarbor provider model without making BaseHarbor the owner of that infrastructure.

The External/BYO flow supports provider registration, inspection, verification and removal while preserving the ownership boundary:

BaseHarbor manages the binding
    !=
BaseHarbor owns the external service

External placement is available for the supported provider families, including PostgreSQL, Valkey, RabbitMQ and MongoDB.

TLS onboarding supports system trust, custom CA material, SAN/wildcard certificates, mTLS references and directory-based certificate discovery. Certificate and private-key material remain deployment/operator state and never become portable Application Intent.

docs.title: Organization and platform configuration
docs.text:
Platform teams can now distribute organization-wide BaseHarbor defaults without changing each application's portable contract.

Organization configuration can provide reusable references for:

  • Stack Profiles;
  • Targets;
  • provider defaults;
  • External/BYO providers;
  • trust and certificate material;
  • policy references.

Configuration can be distributed from local/system sources, Git or OCI artifacts with immutable revision/digest resolution and provenance.

Developer workflows continue to use the normal BaseHarbor commands; organization defaults simply reduce repeated choices where resolution is unambiguous.

docs.title: Provider management surfaces
docs.text:
RabbitMQ, durable Valkey and MongoDB now participate in the same optional management-surface model as existing providers.

Management UIs remain operator/developer surfaces, not application capabilities. They use canonical HTTPS development access and preserve application/shared/external ownership semantics.

docs.title: Provider and contract consistency
docs.text:
The public provider surface now includes the new v0.4.19 capability families across:

  • provider descriptors;
  • Provider SDK/scaffolding;
  • versioned service schemas;
  • Development Adapters;
  • repository inspection;
  • CLI, JSON and MCP surfaces.

This keeps third-party provider implementations aligned with the same capability model used by bundled providers.

docs.title: Runtime and delivery boundaries
docs.text:
v0.4.19 freezes a smaller provider-neutral Runtime boundary that does not require future Kubernetes/OpenShift providers to imitate Docker, Compose or Podman mechanics.

Source/build resolution ends before the Runtime boundary. Runtime providers consume resolved OCI workload artifacts and expose portable lifecycle, observation, readiness, logs, execution and ownership semantics.

Delivery is a separate provider axis with explicit direct versus delegated reconciliation ownership. This keeps future GitOps implementations such as Argo CD or Flux out of portable Application Intent.

The Kubernetes pre-freeze proof was used to verify these boundaries without introducing Kubernetes-specific fields into the portable BaseHarbor contracts.

docs.title: Final stabilization
docs.text:
The release-candidate hardening pass also closes the main developer-journey failures found during v0.4.19 verification:

  • non-interactive CLI and MCP memory-approval semantics now stay consistent and typed;
  • PTY-driven required-secret entry preserves buffered input across multiple prompts;
  • workload failures retain bounded secret-safe diagnostics before cleanup and failed rebuild candidates cannot poison later source-change detection;
  • HTTPS workload contracts fail before mutation when required exposure intent is missing;
  • nested companion applications can be initialized inside an already adopted repository tree;
  • generated Go and Python greenfield workloads start with complete dependency/readiness behavior;
  • destroy and restore no longer leave deployment/provider state that produces empty residue, phantom reconciliation or missing development routes;
  • workspace bootstrap errors and development management credentials are discoverable through normal BaseHarbor UX;
  • the Target/environment development username remains configurable, with developer only as the default.

docs.title: Security
docs.text: v0.4.19 keeps portable intent separate from provider credentials, trust material and runtime ownership state. External/BYO onboarding is binding-management only: BaseHarbor does not claim ownership of external infrastructure, and removal must not destroy it. Shared-provider administration credentials remain separate from application credentials, normal status/doctor/evidence output remains secret-safe, and destructive operations continue to fail closed on ambiguous ownership or unsupported placement.

docs.title: Compatibility
docs.text:
Docker and rootless Podman remain the reference runtimes for v0.4.19.

Kubernetes/OpenShift production support is not introduced by this release. v0.4.19 establishes the contracts required so those providers can be added later without redesigning application or capability semantics.

docs.title: Intentionally deferred
docs.text:
• Kubernetes and OpenShift production Runtime Providers remain future releases; v0.4.19 freezes the provider-neutral contracts they will consume.
  • Delivery-provider implementations such as Argo CD or Flux are not introduced by this release.
  • Broader dynamic provider/plugin loading remains outside the v0.4.19 release boundary.

docs.title: BaseHarbor v0.4.2
docs.text:
BaseHarbor v0.4.2 separates an application's logical resource from the provider instance that happens to serve it.

That distinction lets BaseHarbor reuse infrastructure where sharing is sensible, keep dedicated infrastructure isolated where it matters, and adopt existing external services without pretending BaseHarbor owns them.

The developer workflow stays the same: no Manifest v1 migration is required.

docs.title: Added
docs.text:
BaseHarbor now understands three provider scopes:

  • shared — one BaseHarbor-managed provider can serve multiple applications;
  • application-scoped — a provider belongs to one application and cannot cross that ownership boundary;
  • external — an existing/BYO provider can satisfy a logical resource while its lifecycle stays outside BaseHarbor.

The provider registry is persisted in protected BaseHarbor state and records logical resource-to-provider-instance bindings plus explicit lifecycle ownership.

docs.title: Changed
docs.text:
The current stack now maps naturally to the registry:

OpenBao              -> shared
PostgreSQL instances -> application-scoped
Valkey instances     -> application-scoped

A second application can reuse the same compatible shared provider without BaseHarbor accidentally provisioning a duplicate. Dedicated providers remain isolated to their owning application.

Existing v0.4.1 applications are adopted automatically after the next successful baha app apply or baha app up.

Destroying an application removes its bindings and BaseHarbor-owned application-scoped provider records while shared and external provider instances remain.

docs.title: Security
docs.text:
Provider registry state is written atomically with owner-only permissions and read/modify/write updates are serialized so concurrent BaseHarbor operations cannot silently overwrite each other.

Application-scoped providers fail closed on cross-application binding attempts. Corrupt, duplicate or ambiguous registry state is rejected.

External provider entries use non-secret references only; credentials and secret-bearing connection data remain outside the registry. BaseHarbor never treats an external provider as lifecycle-owned.

docs.title: Deprecated
docs.text: No public baha command or Manifest v1 field is deprecated in v0.4.2.

docs.title: Removed
docs.text: Nothing from the supported v0.4.1 CLI, Manifest v1 or Compose workflow is removed.

docs.title: Compatibility & upgrade notes
docs.text:
No baseharbor.yaml migration is required.

Provider placement remains deployment/operator state and is intentionally not added to portable application intent.

v0.4.2 does not yet add a public provider-selection syntax, replace existing Compose provisioning, or implement Kubernetes/OpenShift/cloud providers. Those remain separate milestones so this release stays focused and compatible.

The practical benefit is architectural but concrete: later shared observability, dedicated databases, customer-managed services and cloud providers can be introduced without changing what the application says it needs.

For detailed technical history, see CHANGELOG.md.

docs.title: BaseHarbor v0.4.20
docs.text:
Status: Work in progress

Release umbrella: #519

docs.title: Highlights
docs.text: v0.4.20 makes repository adoption source-neutral and completes the safe Git workflow for developer workspaces before the v0.5 contract freeze.

docs.title: Adopt more existing repositories
docs.text:
BaseHarbor can inspect and adopt applications described with:

  • Docker Compose;
  • repository-authored Podman Quadlet;
  • raw Kubernetes YAML.

The portable baseharbor.yaml describes logical workload components instead of carrying Compose-specific service or file identity.

This means the same application intent is no longer tied to the syntax used by the repository.

When a repository contains multiple plausible workload sources, BaseHarbor does not guess. Guided adoption asks which source is authoritative and records that repository choice separately from the portable application contract when necessary.

docs.title: Kubernetes repositories can be understood before Kubernetes runtime support
docs.text:
v0.4.20 can inspect and adopt raw Kubernetes manifests without requiring a live cluster.

This release does not add the Kubernetes Runtime Provider. A repository can therefore be understood and adopted even when the currently selected Runtime Provider cannot yet run that workload source. BaseHarbor reports that limitation explicitly instead of silently translating or changing the application.

docs.title: Safer multi-repository workspace updates
docs.text:
The existing multi-repository workspace gains:

baha app workspace status
baha app workspace update --check
baha app workspace update

BaseHarbor uses the installed Git CLI and only performs safe fast-forward updates when the working tree is clean, an upstream exists and history has not diverged.

It does not automatically stash changes, reset worktrees, rebase, merge divergent branches, resolve conflicts or switch branches.

docs.title: Clearer repository inspection
docs.text:
baha app inspect now reports workload-source ambiguity and adoption results consistently across Compose, Quadlet and Kubernetes repositories.

The normal developer flow remains small:

baha app inspect .
baha app init
baha up

docs.title: Not included in v0.4.20
docs.text:
The following remain planned for later releases:

  • Helm workload-source support;
  • Kustomize workload-source support;
  • Kubernetes Runtime Provider;
  • OpenShift Runtime Provider;
  • Argo CD / Flux or generic GitOps delivery.

docs.title: BaseHarbor v0.4.21
docs.text:
Status: Work in progress

Release umbrella: #569

docs.title: Highlights
docs.text: v0.4.21 closes the remaining application-consumption, credential/access and availability semantics before the v0.5 contract freeze.

docs.title: Logical application-to-application consumption
docs.text:
Applications can declare that one logical component consumes an interface exposed by another logical component without embedding Docker, Podman, Kubernetes, OpenShift, namespace, Pod, container or node identity into portable intent.

Same-application and cross-application consumption use the same logical contract. Runtime placement, replica count, rescheduling, rolling replacement and failover do not change the producer/consumer relationship.

docs.title: One explicit credential ownership model
docs.text:
BaseHarbor distinguishes three credential classes consistently:

  • human / management identity;
  • application-service credentials;
  • BaseHarbor-internal machine identity.

Application business users, groups and roles remain application-owned. BaseHarbor does not introduce a parallel business-user or business-RBAC model.

docs.title: Standards-first management access
docs.text:
Managed human-facing surfaces expose an explicit authentication integration class:

  • native OIDC/OAuth2;
  • an existing standards-based authentication adapter;
  • provider-native credentials;
  • unsupported.

The small admin, edit, view, audit role profile applies only to BaseHarbor-managed infrastructure surfaces. Providers report limited or unsupported mappings instead of pretending to enforce finer authorization.

docs.title: Safer secret ownership, projection and rotation
docs.text:
BaseHarbor distinguishes authoritative secret state from runtime projections.

Secret-bearing canonical state remains protected. Runtime-readable files are separate read-only projections where required, while environment variables remain a compatibility delivery mechanism rather than the preferred secret transport.

Interactive secret replacement requires matching hidden confirmation before mutation. Credential and PKI changes use an explicit prepare/reconcile/verify/ retire lifecycle where the selected provider/runtime supports continuity.

docs.title: Portable availability and HA intent
docs.text:
The normal HA decision is intentionally small:

ha: true

Optional sparse overrides can change HA for a specific logical component/capability or request a fixed instance count.

Runtime and capability-provider availability are negotiated independently. If the selected realization cannot satisfy a requested guarantee, BaseHarbor fails before mutation rather than silently downgrading.

Availability is part of the existing Application, Runtime Provider and Capability Provider model; v0.4.21 does not introduce a second HA lifecycle.

docs.title: Provider-native HA and stable endpoints
docs.text:
For managed providers whose v0.4.21 realization is verified, ha: true uses the provider's established availability mechanism rather than duplicating a single-process topology.

Verified provider/runtime work in this release includes:

  • Valkey with a multi-member topology, Sentinel and a stable access endpoint;
  • MongoDB with a replica set behind the stable logical database binding;
  • RabbitMQ with a multi-member cluster, quorum-aware messaging semantics and stable management access;
  • SeaweedFS with a distributed object-storage realization and stable S3/admin access;
  • managed Keycloak with multiple application members, HA PostgreSQL backing, stable issuer/discovery/JWKS/Admin surfaces and credential/signing/admin rotation continuity;
  • OpenTelemetry Collector HA transport;
  • Prometheus HA realization;
  • Loki HA ingestion/query continuity behind a stable access endpoint;
  • Tempo HA ingestion/query continuity across query frontend, distributor and replicated Redpanda-backed ingestion components;
  • the local exposure/developer gateway preserving stable canonical HTTPS routing across backend replacement and configuration/TLS reload.

PostgreSQL/OpenBao control-plane HA remains part of the release acceptance and must be complete before the release is finalized.

docs.title: Honest failure domains
docs.text:
On single-host Docker/Podman, provider HA protects the failure modes the local runtime can honestly survive, such as member/process loss and rolling maintenance inside that runtime host.

It does not claim runtime-host failure tolerance.

The local development/exposure gateway also has one loopback host-port owner. BaseHarbor therefore reports stable routing/hot-reload continuity there without labelling the ingress path as redundant host-level HA.

docs.title: Identity and management continuity
docs.text:
Managed Keycloak keeps one stable issuer/discovery/JWKS contract and stable Admin surface while individual members fail and recover.

The v0.4.21 identity work also verifies client-secret rotation, signing-key rotation and replacement of the managed administrative credential without changing the logical application identity contract.

docs.title: Observability continuity
docs.text:
The shipped observability stack now has explicit HA realization and runtime verification for OpenTelemetry Collector, Prometheus, Loki and Tempo where the selected local runtime/provider combination supports it.

Ingestion/query endpoints remain logical/stable application-facing contracts; member topology remains provider/runtime realization state.

docs.title: Truthful status and evidence
docs.text:
Availability negotiation is surfaced through the same shared semantics used by status, doctor, JSON/MCP and lifecycle evidence.

BaseHarbor distinguishes:

  • requested guarantees;
  • resolved provider/runtime guarantees;
  • satisfied versus unsupported guarantees;
  • explicit non-HA exceptions;
  • failure-domain limits.

A process being RUNNING is never treated as proof that an HA guarantee is satisfied.

docs.title: Upgrade notes
docs.text:
BaseHarbor is still pre-v1 and the v0.5 compatibility freeze has not happened yet. v0.4.21 intentionally replaces incorrect pre-freeze assumptions instead of carrying compatibility shims for behavior that has not been frozen.

Applications should keep portable intent sparse and provider-neutral. Runtime member names, replica identities and provider-native clustering details do not belong in baseharbor.yaml.

docs.title: BaseHarbor v0.4.22
docs.text: Release date: 2026-10-06. Release umbrella: #570. Implementation: #790.

docs.title: Machine operations
docs.text:
Supported business operations share the existing operator authorization boundary across CLI, JSON and MCP. Stable application identity, managed-environment policy, ownership, explicit destructive approval and secret-safe results apply before mutation. Host shell sessions, long-running transports and binary self-replacement remain explicit local modes.

The generated coverage matrix and MCP registry cover discovery and supported operation modes. Automation examples show concrete calls for application intent, workspaces, protected secrets and public host trust.

docs.title: Extension verification and public conformance
docs.text:
Versioned descriptors cover six neutral extension families. Content verification recomputes immutable digests, verifies signatures against operator-configured keys and checks digest-bound in-toto/SBOM/provenance evidence. Verification and publisher/deployment trust policy remain separate; no signer vendor is required. Unavailable evidence never becomes verified evidence.

External implementations can import conformance/provider/v1 and run the public lifecycle or full profile. The full profile reuses the existing harness and adds drift, faults, recovery, foreign ownership, sibling isolation and repeated destroy checks. An independent external module exercises the exported API without internal imports. See artifact trust and public conformance.

docs.title: Repository adoption and lifecycle fixes
docs.text:
• Quick init preserves detected HTTP/HTTPS exposure contracts. Ambiguous target ports fail before the manifest is written.
  • Repeated quick init leaves the existing contract unchanged and reports that result; it does not silently approve repository evolution.
  • Standalone preflight uses the same workload contract gate as lifecycle mutation. Repository up checks that contract before starting the control plane.
  • Configuration records are configured, not applying. Failed apply preflight produces a non-ready failure observation without a successful verification timestamp.
  • Target teardown preserves application intent, source and inputs. It marks a registration not applied only when its application runtime directory and matching runtime containers are absent. Partial or live application state remains available for recovery.
  • Application help lists new once.
  • Generated Go applications import the native clients and TLS helpers required by messaging, document databases and durable key-value storage. Repository capability validation explicitly reports that it has not compiled the project; real builds cover individual and combined capabilities.
  • Control-plane memory planning reads the selected standard or HA topology, includes all members and transient admin/bootstrap services, and labels planning budgets ESTIMATED. Container count is not a measured memory multiplier.
  • Fresh control planes default to one native PostgreSQL server and one OpenBao server with authoritative PostgreSQL storage, TLS and stable endpoints. Explicit HA retains three members. Retained topology conflicts fail before mutation; no pre-freeze migration or legacy compatibility is provided.
  • Shared PostgreSQL follows SQL availability intent: the default is a single native, non-root PostgreSQL service; explicit HA retains the provider-native cluster. A retained provider rejects incompatible member requirements before mutation. Its pre-freeze state contract is replaced directly, without migration or legacy support. Status reports actual members and topology.

Target and installation destruction preview the concrete owned containers, networks and volumes. Resource results and residues are returned through CLI, JSON and MCP. Shared providers are removed after their application consumers are gone; external source/data and recovery files are explicitly preserved. Container removal includes associated anonymous volumes, while declared external volumes remain outside the deletion scope.

docs.title: BaseHarbor v0.4.23
docs.text: Released on 2026-10-08. Release umbrella: #571; implementation: #809.

docs.title: Core installation and first application
docs.text:
BaseHarbor Core provides SQL, Secrets and Identity. The reference providers are PostgreSQL, OpenBao and Keycloak. The Web Console is optional.

Core setup does not require an Application or a repository. It verifies the three capabilities and records an authoritative installation identity and readiness state. A retry reconciles owned resources and preserves that identity; foreign or ambiguous state is refused. Partial failures retain their bootstrap stage for recovery.

When the first application needs a Core, guided setup offers to provision it and continues the original operation after readiness verification. Non-interactive requests return an explicit bootstrap requirement unless automatic setup was requested. CLI, JSON, MCP and protected HTTP use the shared bootstrap semantics.

The development/deployment machine question changes defaults. Development defaults support local repositories and workspaces; deployment defaults require explicit source/workspace selection. Ordinary safe local development does not require an interactive login.

docs.title: Security and placement
docs.text:
Protected credentials and TLS remain part of the Core contract. Core capabilities are mandatory; provider placement may be shared or application-isolated. Additional isolation can add provider instances and resource consumption.

An optional Console connects to one selected Core within the same installation and security boundary. Same-origin HTTPS is the default topology. Browser-origin and destination checks prevent credentials from being forwarded to a foreign Core. Application Identity reconciliation cannot replace installation Identity resources.

Application operations keep Core-managed secrets, service PKI and runtime-permission brokers bound to the selected installation, independently of workload placement. Execution revalidates that Core binding and refuses changed or unavailable configuration before native workload inspection or mutation. Remote selections never fall back implicitly to a local Core.

Generated provider TLS bind files keep the permissions required by their unprivileged native service beneath protected staging directories. Runtime environments remain owner-only. Immutable project verification detects altered file permissions before execution; ordinary destroy retains persistent data, while an explicit owned reset can remove it. Actual remote Application qualification remains required.

Ordinary Podman destroy/reapply retains and reuses the same owned provider data volume. Managed unit removal rechecks native ownership before stopping a service; an old own unit receipt cannot authorize a resource replaced with foreign labels.

The remote Quadlet project adapter publishes the complete graph before activation, starts container dependencies before their dependents, and reverses that order for destruction. Cyclic dependencies are rejected before publication. These project mechanics still require actual remote Application qualification.

Core-managed init services retain native completion evidence. Core verifies successful completion before starting a dependent application; failed or unstarted init services block activation. These managed units are excluded from automatic node startup so a reboot cannot bypass Core verification.

Managed provider publication requires the exact immutable project receipt to be persisted by Core before activation. A failed persistence step leaves no executable handle and does not automatically replay publication. Owned Podman network teardown removes only the exact network without force, preserving live consumers. Explicit provider data reset verifies volume absence and reconciles an explicit retry after ordinary teardown. The focused native provider proof does not replace the complete remote Application journey.

Resource output distinguishes planning estimates from measured observations. No universal Core memory minimum is claimed. Qualification samples the complete PostgreSQL/OpenBao/Keycloak topology, recording stabilized idle usage, sampled startup/convergence peaks, simultaneous totals, provider images and placement. The Core resource observations record the qualified Docker reference topology and its measurement limits.

Remote memory preflight uses fresh available-RAM/swap evidence from the selected authenticated execution node. Core-host RAM and runtime-info totals cannot substitute for node capacity; exhausted RAM is refused even without a reliable workload estimate. This projection does not measure PSI or VM/cgroup limits and does not establish complete remote Application qualification.

docs.title: Managed trust rotation
docs.text: The protected HTTP projection can request the same Core credential and service CA rotation used by CLI/MCP for an explicitly selected installation. The connected Console asks for confirmation; recovery material remains with Core. Rotation returns only verified readiness flags. Interrupted observation must be inspected before retrying, and does not trigger automatic replay. Browser rotation qualification against the final release candidate remains required.

docs.title: v0.4.22 regression fixes
docs.text:
Identity startup authenticates the first Keycloak member before additional members join, preventing concurrent initial database migrations. Core readiness also tolerates transient native authentication-server errors; invalid credentials and other client denials still fail closed.

Interactive terminals preserve early input and terminal protocol replies. Log observations deliver small output chunks promptly, including when following an otherwise idle container. Execution observations preserve idle HTTPS transport during provider setup; keepalive comments do not report progress or extend authentication deadlines. Application repair retains its selected environment. Authenticated operator requests preserve tenant membership resolution across reused database connections without weakening row-level isolation or allowing unscoped writes.

Application overview now consumes the canonical status observations, including managed providers. Backup restores runtime-permission brokers using Core runtime context and attempts bounded recovery after capture cancellation. Closed or non-terminal secret input returns an actionable missing-secret error.

Generated Compose and source consume matching runtime bindings.
