Runtime permission/consumption adapters supply verified DependencyRoots from existing plans to the same resolver. Nil roots with those intents mean incomplete; [] proves no extra provider realization, not absence of security requirements. Each ConsumerIntent supplies its own roots; one consumer cannot borrow another consumer's verification. Unknown roots never authorize a Core-free mutation.

No capability implies the old Core package. SQL, cache, Secrets, Identity and HTTPS select only the realization and its genuine declared dependencies. Identity may need SQL. HTTPS does not automatically need Identity or OpenBao. Independently enabled management/Console services contribute their actual security requirements as separate consumers; TLS/OIDC/mTLS/authorization/HA/recovery are never weakened. The legacy core output classifies an actual declaration, never requests a bundle.

The shared read-only result is baseharbor.footprint/v1:

Field Meaning requirements Requested capability, existing binding or requested/unbound, selected instance/state existing / additional Existing/shared/stopped resources versus declared newly needed resources dependencies Selected dependency IDs; null is unverifiable, [] is verified none unused Informational IDs outside this request and without bindings; never removal authority scope / ownership / shared / consumers Existing ownership and binding count; no invented app counts memory_bytes / containers measured/estimated/unknown; values require nonnegative quantity and source core / complete Actual declared requirement and structural certainty; incomplete forbids unsafe mutation

Unknown measurements may coexist with complete structural resolution. Estimates come from provider evidence, never guessed RAM/container promises or totals.

docs.title: Native backend placement replacement
docs.text:
The existing operator placement policy can switch owned PostgreSQL/Valkey between shared and application-scoped realization through normal app apply. The desired footprint reports the destination as requested/unbound until verified apply publishes its binding. The concrete impact names original and destination owners and explicitly states that destination data is independent: old contents are not automatically copied. Original volumes, protected credentials and registry owners remain; a return to either placement reuses its retained storage. Unknown access or material continuity remains partial and requires the current acknowledgements.

Applied and pending backend placements are realization metadata in the existing deployment GeneratedState, not authored application intent or another registry. Read-only canonical native inventory uses that owner projection, so changed operator policy cannot rewrite the previous realization during retry. An interrupted deployment protects both original and destination providers in the same Target consumer union, even when a sibling uses different current policy. Only actual destination/workload verification and old-runtime convergence permit publishing the new binding and clearing the pending projection. Other consumers retain shared runtime. One shared source split into named destinations is shown with all destination effects rather than a fabricated single replacement.

This native placement path does not implement database content migration, OpenBao/Identity material handoff or unsupported external provider adapters.

Automatic selection retains the deployment's selected placement after a one-shot operator override is removed, including capability disable/re-add. Explicit operator policy requests a new replacement; execution captures that selection and revalidates it against the acknowledged plan. Native PostgreSQL verification uses the retained container role and database. Native Valkey projects its default principal with the retained password; the protected shared ACL identity remains available for a return to shared placement. This principal change is an explicit plan consequence, not a credential reset.

docs.title: Target consumer union and add/remove/re-add
docs.text:
Application --full-reset and remote application destruction acknowledge an aggregate baseharbor.provider-impact-scope/v1 owned by the selected deployment. The embedded provider plan alone cannot authorize deletion of the deployment's protected state. Both current acknowledgements are required; full reset also requires separate data-deletion consent. Changed publication/recovery ownership invalidates that consent. Unverified remote material/access is explicitly partial. Default remote destruction retains the existing publication, credentials and deployment owner, releases references only after verified container removal, and uses the protected retired intent for explicit reactivation. No unauthenticated access or successful material handoff is inferred from retained files.

ResolveProviderPlan(snapshot, consumers, inventoryComplete) delegates every active consumer to ResolveFootprint and unions its full dependency closure. ConsumerIntent is an ephemeral projection of an existing app or independent management owner: Key, Active, Manifest, Preferences, DependencyRoots. Inactive entries retain identity and release bindings. The caller proves complete Target inventory from authoritative existing owners. Unaccounted bindings or unverifiable facts make the plan incomplete. Automatic convergence then preserves resources; intentional changes use the concrete consequence analysis and acknowledgement below.

For an interrupted existing deployment, ConsumerIntent.RetainedIntents may project canonical applied/pending manifests under the SAME active system app ID and environment. Each uses the existing ResolveFootprint and relevant explicit preferences; requirements and provider/dependency closure are deduplicated into one consumer. Retained capability bindings are not released merely because the desired manifest no longer requests them. Runtime roots alone cannot preserve those bindings. The adapter supplies the observed dependency-root union for all canonical projections, including runtime permissions/consumption. Different or missing owners and inactive retained projections are invalid; unknown retained requirements keep inventory incomplete. Only verified lifecycle completion removes the retained projection and permits ordinary last-consumer convergence. No new identity, stored manifest owner or resolver is introduced.

baseharbor.provider-plan/v1 contains per-consumer footprints, required provider IDs, released bindings and ownership/evidence-backed changes:

Action Meaning add Materialize selected newly required realization reuse Keep realization required by an app, management consumer or dependency restart Reactivate an owned stopped required runtime stop Stop owned running runtime after the last consumer releases it remove-runtime Remove unneeded owned stopped runtime, preserving persistent data preserve External/BYO, foreign/unverifiable or incomplete inventory; never implicit deletion

All changes carry PreserveData=true. These are plans, not permissions to invoke runtime mutation directly. Session 2 consumes them through existing plan -> preflight -> confirm -> apply -> verify. Preserve each data/recovery item with an individual reason; deletion requires explicit destructive consent and ownership proof. Automatic convergence preserves shared-still-used resources; intentional owned removal discloses every affected consumer. External/foreign infrastructure is never deleted. Repeat apply, interrupted retry and disable/re-enable converge idempotently. Capability removal belongs to v0.4.25, not a later reclamation project.

CLI/human, JSON and MCP consume the same domain results and existing machine error/exit/authorization mappings. ResolutionError remains typed. Fixtures: internal/application/testdata/v0425-resolution.json; union invariants: internal/application/provider_union_test.go. The full provider/capability wizard is v0.4.26; #777 profile/host contracts below remain specification only.

docs.title: Provider changes: consequences and developer choice
docs.text:
Developers may add, change, replace, disable and remove functionality, including choosing no continuation or complete deletion. Missing alternatives are disclosed consequences, not a permanent policy veto. An alternative-less, unknown or destructive outcome displays Achtung and requires two independently explicit acknowledgements of the concrete current plan. Data deletion additionally needs the existing distinct destructive authorization. Ordinary apply consent does not implicitly acknowledge either stage or delete data.

DescribeProviderChanges(snapshot, union, requests, observation) enriches the same resolved consumer union. It neither resolves another provider graph nor mutates state. Direct provider operations and app/Target lifecycle adapters project their requests into this API. ProviderPlan.Impact carries the shared optional result; CLI, JSON/MCP and the later wizard consume the same baseharbor.provider-impact/v1. The existing plan/preflight/confirmation/apply/verify authorities execute it.

Domain result Required meaning before / after Actual provider kind/instance, Target, scope/owner, locations and safe access/security references; proposed After is not an execution receipt dependencies / dependents / functions Affected apps and independent management/Console consumers; transitive dependency path, required/optional need, lost/changed/remaining function and observed expiry/validation behavior scenario Capability no longer requested; provider removed while still required; replacement; provider still used by another consumer; unused provider materials Individual current material and location, recovery references, intended retained/transferred/deleted/revoked/expired/invalidated/nonrecoverable/unknown disposition and destination/access prerequisites Concrete handoff, rebind or adapter-specific verification, support/evidence and consequence if unverified; no fictional fallback effects Applicable actual before/after availability, consistency, durability, retention, protocol, policy/TLS/HA, delivery, routing, reconnection or recovery changes from the adapter complete Knowledge completeness; false requires Achtung/two acknowledgements and does not prohibit the informed choice plan_id / revision Deterministic digest of consequences plus relevant binding/ownership/dependency state and existing-owner revision; materially changed facts invalidate old consent confirmations_required / destructive One ordinary stage, or two for alternative-less/unknown/destructive effects; explicit data-deletion consent remains separate

ProviderPlan.ConsumerActivity includes explicitly inactive consumers from the same intents; past runtime use is not mistaken for current need. Incidental quantity sampling does not invalidate otherwise identical consequences.

ProviderImpactObservation is an ephemeral projection of existing installation, deployment, runtime, registry, credential, certificate and recovery owners. IntegrationDescriptor.ChangeContract() supplies the shipped provider's function, material and operational inventory requirements. Iterate ReferenceIntegrations(); there is no second provider registry or fixed product warning engine. Unknown extension contracts and missing observations are visibly unknown. They are never reported generically safe or successfully continued.

Consumer-specific Continuations prove a supported replacement and verified rebind. A running compatible replacement by itself is insufficient. Verify secure handoff/access before claiming continued function or deleting the old realization. If no handoff exists, the developer can instead acknowledge the resulting lost function twice and continue the requested removal. Retained inaccessible storage is recovery, not secret delivery, token issuance or certificate renewal. Do not write secrets to plaintext manifests, repositories, logs or an invented fallback. Intentional removal of required authentication shows the affected service/access as unavailable; it never silently enables unauthenticated management.

Only actual OpenBao usages produce secret-policy, dynamic-credential or PKI consequences. Lease expiry/revocation and downstream validity require real evidence; exporting a credential is not continuity proof. Current token/certificate validity is distinct from future issuance, renewal, JWKS refresh, sessions and revocation. Observed offline validation and expiry may produce changed rather than instantly unavailable validation. Do not invent uniformly invalid tokens or certificates. Caches, jobs, sessions, queues and telemetry buffers are not automatically considered disposable. Unknown retention/location remains unknown. Retained material stays at its actual location; deleted material says no destination; deletion. Ownership and authorized references must be proven by existing owners. Two acknowledgements grant no authority over somebody else's external resources.

Multiple changes form one aggregate plan. Removing a replacement's dependency invalidates its continuation; stopping SQL identifies dependent Identity/broker functions. Scoped unbinding preserves the other consumers' runtime and reports which consumer loses access. Automatic last-consumer convergence preserves data; explicit fully destructive requests inventory every affected item before consent.

ValidateProviderChangeConsent checks both stages, current plan digest and separate deletion consent. Existing interactive and noninteractive authority adapters collect acknowledgements; the interactive adapter asks separately for data deletion after the required plan acknowledgements. Declining that question or reaching EOF does not authorize deletion. Machine consent supplies delete_data independently. No extra CLI flags or independent frontend policy engine. Always replan from current authoritative observations immediately before mutation. A stale plan must be displayed and acknowledged again. Technical inability to execute an unsupported handoff is reported honestly, not disguised as successful relocation.

RecordProviderChangeResult accepts actual verified execution outcomes, reports complete/partial/failed state, actual final locations and every pending operation. Actual affected-function outcomes require their own consumer/root/function verification and evidence; a runtime stop alone is not a login/lease/PKI receipt. It never copies proposed After into an accomplished result. Missing material, changed disposition or missing recovery evidence remains a partial failure. PendingProviderChanges preserves the original consumer scope and returns only unfinished operations/material actions for the existing idempotent replan/retry lifecycle. It is not a scheduler or new persistence authority. Interrupted handoff, rollback/reconnection work and irreversible effects remain visible in receipts.

docs.title: Global registration changes across Targets
docs.text:
A global external-provider registration has its existing registration owner, not an invented runtime Target. ComposeProviderImpactScope composes unchanged ProviderImpactPlan outputs for every observed Target. The adapter inventories configured and retained Target state, applied and interrupted deployment bindings, and independent management consumers before declaring the scope complete. This projection performs no additional resolution and creates no state owner.

The aggregate PlanID binds the registration owner/content revision, all Target plans and their actual consequences. Leaf consent cannot approve the whole scope; changed registration, Target membership, binding or consequence requires fresh consent. Countdown samples alone do not invalidate unchanged absolute validity. Unknown/incomplete or destructive scope shows Achtung and uses the same two acknowledgements and separate destructive consent as single-Target changes.

ProviderScopeOwner.destructive marks permanent deletion of the aggregate owner itself, including installation configuration/state when no provider leaf exists. It contributes to the scope revision and requires separate delete_data consent in addition to both current-plan acknowledgements. Omitting this optional field retains the existing non-destructive owner semantics.

RecordProviderImpactScopeResult validates each Target's execution through the existing receipt authority. Registration-entry deletion alone never proves consumer reconfiguration or all-Target success. Missing/unknown owner or Target receipts remain partial; preserved registration/ownership supports fresh replan and retry. External infrastructure, data and credentials remain outside local registration-removal authority. The runtime/transport adapter must still observe, authorize, revalidate, execute and verify each requested operation.

docs.title: Existing ancillary realizations
docs.text:
ResolutionSnapshot.Ancillary observes existing gateway/sidecar realizations from runtime/route owners. ProviderFact.Ancillary and OwnerReference identify them; ProviderFootprint and impact realizations retain that distinction. This is an ephemeral inventory alongside the existing registry, not another registration or state owner. Ancillary Provider.Capabilities is empty: Automatic does not offer these as application providers, and explicit capability selection is incompatible. The same dependency closure includes their actual IDs only through verified provider dependencies or consumer roots. The same union accounts for shared users, owned retirement, unknown state and impact. No unconditional sidecar/Core package.

A Target-owned shared gateway uses its real existing installation/route owner and no fabricated application UUID. It does not claim that Caddy's selectable provider integration supports generic Shared placement. App sidecars retain their actual system-owned app ID. The native executor uses Shared scope and its single existing Target project owner (RuntimeExecutorDependency); every app/management root references that same physical ID. It is never owned by one app or counted through independent app aliases. The per-app broker uses Application scope.

Ordinary declared workload components use distinct runtime-workload ancillary metadata (RuntimeWorkloadDependency), including zero-capability apps. They are not privileged executors or selectable capability providers. Actual run/access, in-flight work, configuration and volume consequences require observation; a matching project label does not authorize an undeclared component. Runtime broker/executor metadata describes actual authorization, credential, execution/control and in-flight effects; usages still require observation.

docs.title: Shipped provider coverage
docs.text:
This is the inventory of declaration-level coverage. The adapter must provide actual data/access locations and usage; the material kinds below are potential inventory categories, not assertions that every instance has every item. Runtime entry-point coverage and native acceptance belong to the consuming lifecycle tests. Existing runtime-broker/runtime-executor sidecars have ancillary-only consequence metadata, not shipped selectable capability integrations. Undeclared extension contracts remain unknown.

Registered provider Relevant functions/material inventory Location/access authority and specific consequences PostgreSQL Transactions/queries; database, schemas, WAL, credentials, backups Existing database/runtime/recovery owners; transactions, consistency, durability, reconnect and recovery Valkey Cache/durable KV, actual sessions/jobs; snapshots/AOF Existing runtime/data owners; expiry/eviction, durability and meaningful transient loss OpenBao Actual secret/policy, lease and PKI usage; secrets, keys/certificates, recovery Existing credential/OpenBao/PKI owners and selected backing store; secure delivery, renewal, revocation and expiry Caddy HTTP routing and actual TLS/renewal; routes/configuration, keys/certificates Existing exposure/PKI/runtime owners; DNS/routes, HTTPS availability and future renewal SeaweedFS Object read/write; objects/files, metadata, credentials, backups Existing S3/runtime/recovery owners; durability, S3 compatibility, permissions and retention OpenTelemetry Collector Receive/forward; actual buffers/configuration Existing telemetry/runtime owners; forwarding gaps, buffer loss, routing and retention External OTLP Actual receive/forward and registered references External registration/access owner; unbind/rebind effects only, no foreign infrastructure deletion Prometheus Ingest/query and actual rules; metrics, WAL, configuration Existing metrics/runtime/data owners; scrape gaps, retention, query access and recovery Loki Ingest/query; logs, WAL/index, configuration Existing logs/runtime/storage owners; delivery gaps, retention and query access Tempo Ingest/query; traces, WAL/index, configuration Existing traces/runtime/storage owners; delivery gaps, retention and query access Keycloak Actual login/SSO, issuance/validation/JWKS, sessions/refresh; users/realms/clients/signing keys/tokens Existing Identity/database/access owners; login/refresh, cached validity and authenticated management availability External OIDC Actual OIDC consumers and registered references External registration/access owner; local binding removal, no foreign user/realm destruction RabbitMQ Actual queue/pubsub/stream users; messages/in-flight, offsets/topology/credentials Existing messaging/runtime/storage owners; ordering, acknowledgements, delivery, durability and reconnect Ancillary runtime broker Actual authorization/credentials/policy; configuration, certificates/recovery Existing broker/runtime/credential owners; authorization, renewal, TLS and availability Ancillary runtime workload Actual component run/access; in-flight/configuration and volumes Existing application/deployment owner; outage/reconnect and observed material retention, never privileged executor authority Ancillary runtime executor Actual execute/observe/control; in-flight/configuration, certificates/credentials Existing executor/runtime owners; in-flight work, authorization/TLS and reconnect MongoDB Read/write/transactions; documents/indexes/oplog, credentials/backups Existing document/runtime/storage/recovery owners; consistency, durability, protocol and reconnect

Fixtures: internal/application/testdata/v0425-provider-impact.json and v0425-provider-impact-consent.json. Domain tests cover every registered provider, negative ownership/unknown state, cross-provider and two-app/Console effects, replacement verification, aggregate dependency removal, scoped retry, actual final and partial dispositions. Offline schemas validate identical machine results and reject secret-content fields or one-stage unknown/destructive acknowledgements. The complete capability/provider wizard remains v0.4.26.

docs.title: Derived consumer actions and lifecycle coverage
docs.text:
The lifecycle matrix covers all declared functions and material kinds for all fourteen reference integrations, for add/resume/update, stop, destroy, remove-runtime, disable/unbind, rebind and replacement. External runtime mutation is rejected for lack of authority; an intentional local loss of access remains possible. Declaration tests are not native execution acceptance.

ProviderImpactObservation.ConsumerActions projects supported operations of the existing consumer adapter. ProviderChangeRequest.ConsumerActions explicitly selects their IDs. Each action identifies consumer/root/function, actual modes, selected function outcome, dependencies, credential references and locations, and credential owner, synchronization and rotation before/after. An unselected local authentication mode never becomes a fallback. Unsupported/unverified actions remain unknown and can be explicitly accepted; they are never reported working. Selected action dependencies are checked through the existing transitive provider graph on the actual Target. A stopped, removed, foreign, unobserved or cyclic prerequisite, or an unknown dependency closure, makes continuation unknown even when the action's directly named provider is running. Aggregate changes cannot claim continuity through a dependency they interrupt. Replacement providers use the same check for their entire dependency closure. Each node must be registered or canonically ancillary on the selected Target, observed running, supported and verified with realization evidence; a running fact without that observation is insufficient. A planned add/resume does not prove executed availability. Reobserve after actual recovery and acknowledge the fresh plan before claiming continuation. Unverified replacement remains partial and can still be deliberately accepted with the required confirmations. Credential references stay identical unless their change is explicitly selected. Adapters additionally verify that retained values and established synchronization remain consistent; this pure result neither reads nor regenerates passwords. OIDC ownership is distinct from native database/service credentials. For example, Prometheus uses existing devaccess credentials and native basic authentication; SeaweedFS keeps native admin references in its existing protected runtime owner. Identity removal must not reset either merely because an issuer disappears.

ObservedAt and actual ValidUntil/ExpiresAt derive remaining_validity_seconds for tokens, certificates and leases. Missing current validity evidence stays unknown; expired offline validation is unavailable. Retained certificate files imply neither indefinite TLS nor future renewal.

Protected X.509 files expose valid_from and expires_at from the parsed certificates. A bundle uses the latest start and earliest expiry of every certificate, including when a key block precedes them. The current observation distinguishes not-yet-valid, within-window and expired material. This proves time bounds only; chain trust, revocation, endpoint access and future renewal still need actual verification. Key contents and certificate subjects are not emitted.

The consent digest ignores only the changing remaining-validity countdown; absolute expiry, actual expired/valid consequences and changed material still require fresh consent. ProviderMaterial.Retention separately verifies survival of stop and runtime removal for meaningful transient state: cache, sessions, jobs, queues/messages, in-flight work, telemetry buffers, leases and tokens. A volume alone is insufficient; verified loss is individually nonrecoverable and requires destructive consent.

Actual execution receipts must account for each affected function, selected consumer action and operational effect. Missing reconfiguration or changed owner, credential reference, synchronization, rotation or guarantee remains partial/failed. Retry retains selected consumer actions and obtains consent against the fresh plan. A material step is complete for retry only when its verified disposition, final location, delivery/access references and preserved recovery references all match; the correct destination alone cannot hide an incomplete secure handoff. Final receipts and retry exclusion use the same material checks. An unknown material disposition remains unfinished even when the adapter verifies that uncertainty; acknowledging the change does not establish material completion. Incomplete authoritative inventory keeps the overall receipt partial, including when no known operation remains. Verified individual operations are still applied and excluded from replay; the existing lifecycle must observe and replan the unknown inventory before it can establish overall completion. Recovery references follow explicitly selected owned backup transfers/deletions across the aggregate plan. A complete owned deletion may include its inventoried backups with destructive consent; unselected or foreign recovery stays protected.

Provider and existing implementation authority Necessary provider-specific analysis/actions for add/change/remove PostgreSQL — application/runtime_postgres.go, shared_postgres_* Actual SQL consumers and Identity/backing-store dependents; provision/bind and verify access; version/protocol/transactions/WAL/backup consistency; reconnect dependent consumers after selected restore/replacement; distinguish preserved database from lost endpoint Valkey — application/shared_core_valkey.go, valkey_stable_verify.go, valkey_ha*, valkey_credential_rotation* Persistence/AOF/snapshot configuration versus cache/session/job semantics; verify access and actual expiry; rebind clients, preserve credentials; do not treat in-memory sessions/jobs as a preserved volume OpenBao — openbao/managed_credentials.go, service_pki*, runtime_pki*, application dynamic-secret operations Enumerate actual KV/policy/lease/PKI consumers and backing SQL; selected secure delivery handoff with permissions/encryption checks; preserve/revoke credentials deliberately; inventory certificate/key locations, remaining validity, renewal and revocation dependencies; reconfigure each selected consumer before teardown Keycloak — identityprovider/keycloak_files.go, keycloak_driver.go, application/identity_binding.go Actual shared SQL, gateway and OIDC consumers; realm/client/key/session inventory; supported login configuration change and access verification; distinguish offline token validity from JWKS/refresh/issuance; preserve separately owned native service credentials External OIDC — identityprovider external realization and existing registration/binding owner Verify issuer/discovery/client compatibility and every selected consumer mode; remove local bindings only; no authority over foreign accounts, sessions or signing keys Caddy — devgateway/render.go, application exposure and PKI owners Actual app/shared route users, DNS/endpoints, certificate/key references and renewal owner; verify selected routes/TLS/auth access; distinguish retained certificate validity from provider renewal and preserve unrelated routes SeaweedFS — objectstorage/admin_credentials.go, pki_rotation.go, provider realization Actual objects/files/metadata and S3 consumers; consistency/durability/permissions and selected handoff; preserve native admin/client credentials; verify TLS reload, endpoint rebinding and object access RabbitMQ — application/rabbitmq_credentials.go, rabbitmq_ha*, credential rotation and verification Actual queues/streams/topology, offsets, unacknowledged messages and jobs; ordering/delivery/acknowledgement and durable-versus-transient survival; preserve separate application/admin accounts; reconnect and verify publish/consume after change MongoDB — application/mongodb_runtime.go, mongodb_ha*, credential rotation and verification Actual documents/indexes/oplog and clients; protocol/transactions/consistency/durable data; preserve credentials, rebind clients and verify read/write and selected recovery OTel Collector — telemetry realization, application telemetry binding and PKI reload Actual receive/forward destinations, buffers and TLS references; delivery gaps/backpressure or irrecoverable buffered telemetry; configure and verify new routing before claiming downstream delivery External OTLP — existing registered endpoint and telemetry binding owner Protocol/TLS/auth and chosen forwarding endpoint; verify consumer rebinding and delivery; disclose gaps; no mutation/deletion of foreign buffers/stores Prometheus — metrics/prometheus_files.go, prometheus_shared.go, topology/recovery owner Actual scrape/query/rule users, TSDB/WAL and retention; preserve native basic-auth credentials independently of Identity; verify selected config, authentication and query access; disclose scrape gaps and lost alerts Loki — logs/render.go, topology and PKI reload owner Actual log delivery/query consumers, store/index/WAL, labels/protocol/retention; rebind writers/readers and verify access/TLS; disclose log gaps and retained-but-inaccessible history Tempo — traces/tempo_ha.go, topology and PKI reload owner Actual trace ingest/query consumers, buffers/store/index and retention; rebind delivery/query routes and verify TLS/access; distinguish sampling/delivery gaps from deleted history Ancillary broker/executor — runtimebroker/compose_render.go, existing executor/runtime owners Existing policy, service credentials/certificates and in-flight control/work consumers; authorization and expiry/renewal dependencies; verify selected reconnect/control operation; never register these sidecars as new capability offers

The same dependency graph propagates database, gateway, secret/PKI and authentication changes to every actual direct and transitive consumer. Selected transition dependencies are evaluated against aggregate changes: removing the newly selected mode's dependency cannot be reported as a working continuation. Runtime mutation path inventory and native proof of these actions are Session 2's acceptance duty.

docs.title: #777 portable connection-profile transport (contract only)
docs.text:
This is an import/export transport envelope for later #777 implementation, not a replacement for existing development.StackProfile (development/v1), Target configuration, access storage or provider registry. No implementation, file creation or onboarding UI is delivered by this specification.

Envelope field Contract version Exact baseharbor.connection-profile/v1; reject unsupported versions name Human alias; never an identity or authorization claim core.installation_id / core.url Existing canonical Core UUID and HTTPS management endpoint; verify server identity trust.ca_pem / trust.sha256 One public PEM CA certificate and its DER SHA-256 fingerprint; verify agreement and require an independently authorized trust decision targets List of portable descriptors: name, tenant_id, runtime_provider, scope; retain existing Target semantics access OIDC issuer, client_id and scopes only; no imported authorization claims expires_at Optional transport expiry; reject expired enrollment material extensions Namespaced future optional fields; no change to existing required semantics

An example transport describes a Core, trust and selected Targets; it does not contain application intent, provider credentials or a new authoritative state. Targets reference a Core where applicable; profiles are not Targets and do not merge dev/prod installations. Core-less local operation needs no imported profile.

Exclude passwords, private keys, refresh/access tokens, AppRole secrets, recovery material, local sockets/engine contexts, checkout paths and local state roots. Authentication/enrollment artifacts use existing protected access owners after explicit login/enrollment; importing descriptors cannot grant a role, claim a foreign deployment, activate arbitrary endpoints or start resources. Imported public trust alone cannot self-authorize a server. Verify Core UUID, HTTPS, issuer, tenant and selected Target before writing existing config/access owners.

Import is parse -> validate -> resolve references/conflicts -> show diff -> explicit authorization -> existing owner transaction -> verification. Same identity plus same content is idempotent; same alias with another identity is a conflict. Partial writes must be rolled back or exposed as incomplete with a recovery action, never reported as successful. Export is read-only and preserves portable identity without secret/local fields. Host-local values are resolved after import through existing local config. Implementations arrive in later releases and require schema/transaction conformance against these semantics.

docs.title: Host Platform boundary (contract only)
docs.text:
The semantic boundary baseharbor.host-platform/v1 is adapter capability negotiation, not a new runtime, registry, scheduler or multi-OS implementation.

Responsibility Boundary Platform/feature detection Host facts and supported/unsupported/unverifiable outcome with evidence Engine selection Actual runtime endpoint, context and rootless/rootful mode; no silent fallback to privileged engine Local paths / source access Host-local mapping stays outside portable manifest/profile; deterministic failure for unavailable source Credential / trust access Existing protected owner and explicit trust changes; no automatic security downgrade Browser / PTY / shell Host operation support and typed unavailable result; preserve non-TTY/EOF/cancel contracts Runtime execution Existing RuntimeProvider owns workload lifecycle and provider verification Enrollment / remote authority Existing Core/Node authority and mTLS; local host adapter cannot mint remote authority

Linux, WSL2 and Darwin implementations are later releases. Adapters report real support instead of pretending an unsupported host operation succeeded. Host paths, sockets and platform defaults must not change ApplicationID, capability intent, Target ownership, footprint evidence or machine error semantics. No host probing with persistent effects from inspection/footprint.

Normative offline schemas: contracts/footprint/v1/footprint.schema.json and contracts/connection-profile/v1/profile.schema.json. Profile shape validation never proves valid CA material, fingerprint agreement, expiry, tenant uniqueness or authorization; later importers must enforce these semantic checks and allow only reviewed non-secret extensions.

docs.title: Local workload authorization
docs.text:
A portable test or prod environment does not by itself request operator OIDC. An actual local CLI/JSON or local stdio invocation may use verified local-runtime authority for one application operation on one Target and environment. The adapter observes the selected local Docker engine/binding or native rootless Linux Podman info selection. This authority is invocation context, not an OIDC principal, portable input or another identity registry.

Explicit stored/environment operator OIDC policy, an independent management installation (including a valid partial owner), tenant scope, remote execution and HTTP retain their existing authenticated boundaries. HTTP strips inherited local authority. Unknown engine/owner state never fabricates a local proof. Application authorization may provision its genuine provider dependencies; explicit management commands keep their own authorization. Local authority does not grant provider-change confirmations or destructive data consent. The two current-plan acknowledgements remain separate.

The implementation has domain/adapter negative tests. Actual local production CLI and stdio runtime acceptance remains required on the qualified candidate.

docs.title: Fresh execution dependencies and credential delivery
docs.text:
ProviderImpact.ContinuationDependencies binds the selected replacement and consumer actions to the existing Target graph, including transitive ancillary owners. ProviderExecutionOutcome.ContinuationDependencies supplies fresh observations of the same identities and edges after execution. Missing, stopped, unsupported, unverified, foreign or changed owners/edges cannot be reported as a completed continuation. ObserveProviderContinuationDependencies is read-only; it consumes existing registry/ancillary facts and observations, never schedules recovery or creates another state owner. A changed graph needs fresh replan/consent. Failed result evidence remains visible and pending retry.

Native provider observations require every selected canonical container to be present and running, with healthy status when a health check exists. A single running HA member does not qualify the whole declared module. This observation proves process/health inventory only, not quorum, authenticated access, data continuity or unlisted sidecar completeness.

Canonical profile-only recovery helpers are retained in the complete owned inventory but are not continuously required processes. One-shot prerequisites declared with service_completed_successfully and restart: no require actual successful completion instead of running state. Docker verifies the owned exited container; Quadlet may retain that evidence in its current canonical systemd unit after removing the container. Missing, failed, foreign, stale or overridden completion evidence leaves availability unverified. Observing completion never starts or repairs a task, and full lifecycle resource selection remains unchanged.

Normal reapply must not regenerate a missing credential in an existing protected native credential group. SQL, Valkey, RabbitMQ, MongoDB and S3 groups, their independent logical instances and supported management credentials are checked before initial-value generation. Existing runtime declarations, binding material or retained group keys distinguish continuation from a new independent group. Incomplete retained material requires recovery through its original owner; the failed reapply leaves the owner unchanged and never includes secret values in diagnostics. New independent instances and intentional capability retirement remain possible. This guard does not prove live authentication, migrate data or provide a replacement authentication mode.

External OIDC reapply without repeated secret/CA inputs reuses protected material only for the same provider, issuer and client. It does not regenerate credentials, forward them to another authority or silently change a confidential client to a public client. A different authority requires explicit replacement material where retained confidential credentials/trust exist. Unsupported credential/trust removal remains an explicit technical limitation; it does not assert that a public-client or system-trust fallback was implemented.

Identity binding verification compares the host and workload client/credential/ trust projections with runtime and application environment references. Divergence or stale references are failures without secret values in errors. This proves consistent delivery, not user login, token/refresh validity, revocation or future renewal. Their actual access checks remain separate requirements.

docs.title: Installation destruction child authority
docs.text: The installation consequence scope contains each selected application reset scope. The aggregate acknowledgements and separate data decision delegate only to those exact destructive application-deployment scopes after revalidation. They cannot authorize another operation, a changed owner, an undisplayed child or an unknown child scope. Aggregate revision uses semantic child scope IDs rather than live footprint samples. A failed child retains its affected Target and protected retry owner; lower fallback or Target cleanup cannot bypass that child authority. Native operation failures remain partial failures requiring a fresh observed plan and acknowledgements before retry.

docs.title: Control-plane runtime
docs.text: BaseHarbor exposes its protected control-plane API through the baha serve process. The server is deliberately separate from application service protocols: PostgreSQL, Valkey, OpenBao and future S3-compatible services remain directly consumable through their native interfaces.

docs.title: Startup contract
docs.text:
baha serve fails closed before opening the listener unless all required runtime dependencies can be constructed:

  • the control-plane PostgreSQL DSN is configured and reachable
  • the configured OIDC issuer is HTTPS and discovery succeeds
  • at least one OIDC audience is configured
  • the TLS certificate and private key are both present and form a usable key pair
  • authentication, tenant resolution, RBAC, application ownership and application-secret handlers can be composed

The server never falls back to an unauthenticated or plaintext API listener when one of these requirements is missing.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
The current runtime configuration is explicit process configuration:

BASEHARBOR_API_DATABASE_URL
BASEHARBOR_API_OIDC_ISSUER
BASEHARBOR_API_OIDC_AUDIENCES
BASEHARBOR_API_TLS_CERT_FILE
BASEHARBOR_API_TLS_KEY_FILE
BASEHARBOR_API_LISTEN_ADDR

BASEHARBOR_API_OIDC_AUDIENCES is a comma-separated list. BASEHARBOR_API_LISTEN_ADDR defaults to 127.0.0.1:8443 when omitted.

Secret-bearing database URLs must be injected through the runtime environment or another trusted process boundary and must not be committed to source control.

docs.title: HTTP boundaries
docs.text:
The runtime exposes:

GET /healthz
/api/v1/...

/healthz is an unauthenticated process-liveness endpoint and does not expose configuration or dependency details.

Every /api/ request passes through the mandatory security chain:

TLS
  -> bearer token parsing
  -> OIDC discovery/JWKS-backed token verification
  -> identity-scoped membership resolution under PostgreSQL RLS
  -> tenant context
  -> RBAC
  -> authoritative application ownership
  -> protected application API

The current protected API surface contains the application-secret endpoints. Secret values are never exposed through a reveal endpoint.

docs.title: TLS scope
docs.text:
This runtime consumes an already prepared certificate/key pair. Certificate issuance, ACME, internal PKI, BYOC discovery, chain construction and renewal belong to the dedicated certificate-management milestone and are intentionally not implemented here.

The server requires TLS and uses TLS 1.2 or newer. A missing or invalid certificate/key pair prevents startup.

docs.title: Shutdown
docs.text: The main baha process converts SIGINT and SIGTERM into context cancellation. baha serve then performs a bounded graceful HTTP shutdown before closing its PostgreSQL pool.

docs.title: Core provider update contract — v0.4.24
docs.text: Status: implemented; real-version runtime qualification pending. This document describes required behavior, not proof of a supported end-to-end provider upgrade.

docs.title: Authority and boundaries
docs.text:
A selected BaseHarbor release must own immutable provider image digests, versions, compatibility metadata and the complete SQL / Secrets / Identity reference set. No mutable latest resolution is permitted. The immutable catalog is embedded in internal/coreupdate/releases/v0.4.24.json; runtime inventory must match the selected catalog, including dedicated Keycloak backing SQL.

The Core update domain is implemented in internal/coreupdate. It operates on owned realizations, not merely provider types: installation, placement scope, instance and owner form the identity. An external or foreign provider must not be changed automatically.

The planner distinguishes:

  • no_change: version, image and digest all identical;
  • safe_reconcile: an explicitly proven compatible stateless path;
  • backup_recovery_required: a supported data-bearing path with a verified recovery point;
  • migration_required: a supported schema/data migration with explicit verification and recovery requirements;
  • unsupported: refuse before mutation and report the actionable reason.

A PostgreSQL major version change is currently unsupported by the generic planner: it needs a separately proven, provider-native migration path. Image replacement alone is never evidence that data was upgraded.

docs.title: Transaction semantics
docs.text:
1. Resolve the exact BaseHarbor release and all Core expected digests.
  2. Inspect installed owned shared and application-isolated realizations; discover any external providers without taking ownership.
  3. Compute the plan and preflight all changes before mutation.
  4. Require verified recovery-point hooks for every data-bearing upgrade.
  5. Apply through the existing provider-native Core lifecycle and persist stage/result evidence.
  6. Probe actual SQL, Secrets and Identity usability, not merely container readiness.
  7. Resume incomplete owned state idempotently. Never promise rollback for irreversible data migrations.
  8. Report success only when every affected realization and Core semantics verify successfully.

docs.title: Explicit HA point recovery
docs.text:
baha update --recover --version VERSION --yes restores the selected owned Core's PostgreSQL and etcd DCS to the verified update backup point. It does not install a release or replace the CLI. Transactions after that backup point are not included; an update failure never triggers this data rewind automatically.

Recovery holds the Core lifecycle lock, validates Core/Target/release identity, checks immutable physical and DCS artifacts, and rejects credential/environment drift. PostgreSQL writers are stopped before the old DCS. The new DCS starts from the verified isolated restore; the PostgreSQL primary is seeded through a stream into a separate owned volume, and replicas rebuild into separate empty volumes. Actual mounts, mTLS DCS identity/quorum, SQL authentication, Patroni health and replication must verify before commit. Original volumes and the prior manifest are retained.

A committed replay verifies the active cluster without recreating members or replaying extraction. Ambiguous fencing, partial volume seeding or interrupted commit requires reconciliation; it never reactivates both old and new data. A subsequent update uses a new transaction directory without renaming the active DCS bind directories. Existing plaintext DCS installations and PostgreSQL major migrations remain unsupported.

The isolated acceptance gate exercises replica-first replacement and switchover with the same pinned image, a failed replica, real PostgreSQL WAL/SQL restoration, live DCS cutover, original-volume preservation and committed replay. This does not by itself certify compatibility of another Spilo/PostgreSQL image or a full provider-version migration.

docs.title: Human and machine parity
docs.text: baha update --check, human update output, JSON, MCP and protected HTTP must be projections of the same plan/result domain. The existing self-update implementation only handles binary/release assets and MUST NOT report a complete Core upgrade until the provider update integration and semantic verification are present.

docs.title: Release evidence required
docs.text:
• Immutable provider set and installed-version discovery
  • No restart for unchanged realizations
  • PostgreSQL compatible upgrade, plus fail-closed unsupported major upgrade
  • OpenBao sealed/unsealed and recovery state preservation
  • Keycloak post-migration authentication/issuer verification
  • Shared updated exactly once; isolated handled independently
  • Foreign provider untouched
  • Injected partial failure and retry, without duplicated state
  • Docker rootless and Podman rootless runtime proof
  • Evidence bound to the release candidate SHA and provider digests

The initial planner and hook tests prove only contract behavior; they do not qualify the real provider mutation paths.

docs.title: Native provider admission
docs.text:
The manager AppRole deliberately excludes OpenBao's default policy. Its scoped manager policy must grant update on sys/capabilities-self so preflight can inspect its own application-policy rights. No authority to inspect other tokens is granted. Existing installations whose manager policy lacks this endpoint must have an authorized administrator reconcile that narrow policy before upgrading; Core refuses before provider mutation and never recreates a root token or silently broadens its authority.

OpenBao accepts strictly newer patches in the same major/minor stream; the candidate targets 2.7.1. Keycloak follows that same patch rule for HA. The explicitly admitted single-Core 26.7.5 → 26.8.0 path stops/recreates the one member and uses verified SQL/configuration backup and recovery. Other minor/major paths are refused before mutation. A completed native transaction verifies the unchanged immutable inventory and registered application Secret scopes; the narrower binary-only admission rule is not reused to reject those already verified applications.

docs.title: Scope
docs.text:
This specification defines the normative BaseHarbor credential taxonomy and ownership boundary.

It classifies credential material and identity used by BaseHarbor-managed infrastructure. It does not create a new IAM, RBAC, secret-store or provider protocol.

The taxonomy applies consistently across provider implementations, management surfaces, secure bindings, CLI, machine JSON, MCP, status, doctor and evidence.

docs.title: A. Human / management identity
docs.text:
Class A represents infrastructure-facing human access only.

Examples include managed Identity login, provider/management GUIs, and BaseHarbor-managed infrastructure roles.

The portable infrastructure-management role profile is:

admin
edit
view
audit

These roles MUST NOT become application business roles.

docs.title: B. Application-service credentials
docs.text:
Class B represents technical credentials used by an application to consume a capability.

Examples include PostgreSQL, Valkey/cache, RabbitMQ/messaging, MongoDB/document database, object storage/S3 and technical application client secrets.

Class B credentials remain scoped to the application, environment and logical resource as required by the capability contract. They MUST NOT be treated as human identity.

docs.title: C. BaseHarbor-internal machine identity
docs.text:
Class C represents internal machine identity and control credentials.

Examples include mTLS private keys, SPIFFE/workload identities, runtime broker tokens, OpenBao AppRoles, provider-control/provider-admin credentials and internal service-to-service credentials.

Class C credentials MUST remain isolated and MUST NOT inherit or reuse shared human/developer credentials or application-service credentials.

docs.title: Application business identity is out of scope
docs.text:
Application business users, groups, roles and permissions are owned by the application and its selected identity provider.

BaseHarbor MUST NOT maintain a parallel application-user database or proprietary business-RBAC model.

Applications may use normal OIDC, OAuth2, claims, groups, client roles or another selected external identity system.

docs.title: Development
docs.text:
• Class A MAY use one Target-scoped developer-facing credential across compatible BaseHarbor-managed non-OIDC surfaces where technically safe.
  • Native OIDC/OAuth2 remains preferred when a surface supports it.
  • Class B MAY use simple or shared defaults only when application/environment/resource scope and required isolation remain correct.
  • Class C MUST remain isolated.

docs.title: Test and production
docs.text:
• Class A SHOULD use central managed Identity/OIDC where supported.
  • Class A MUST default to isolated per-surface credentials when OIDC is unavailable.
  • Class B MUST default to isolated least-privilege credentials.
  • Explicit supported sharing MAY be selected only when the provider can preserve the required authorization, ownership and isolation semantics.
  • Class C MUST remain isolated.

docs.title: Ownership and sharing rules
docs.text:
Credential sharing is a policy decision only within the same credential class.

A Human / management
    != B Application-service
    != C BaseHarbor-internal machine

Sharing MUST NOT collapse class boundaries.

A shared development credential MUST NOT replace provider-control, workload identity, runtime-broker, AppRole or other machine credentials.

Shared provider infrastructure MUST NOT imply shared Class B credentials between applications.

docs.title: Provider requirements
docs.text:
Provider implementations MUST consume this taxonomy instead of inventing provider-local credential classes.

Provider behavior MUST preserve credential class, owner, application/environment/resource scope where applicable, isolation requirements, authoritative secret-source semantics, projection/delivery semantics, and rotation/revocation semantics.

A provider MUST report an unsupported or limited mapping explicitly rather than silently weakening the requested security semantics.

docs.title: Management surface boundary
docs.text:
Human authentication for BaseHarbor-managed management surfaces belongs to Class A.

Provider administration credentials used internally by BaseHarbor belong to Class C.

A provider-native username/password used directly by a human as the effective management login belongs to Class A even when the provider stores it in its native credential system.

docs.title: Secure-binding boundary
docs.text:
secure-binding/v1 remains the workload/capability security and lifecycle binding contract.

It carries provider-neutral references and security metadata for Class B and Class C material when that material participates in workload/capability binding.

It does not become a human-login or business-RBAC contract.

Plaintext secret values remain forbidden in portable intent, provider registry state, plan, status, doctor, evidence and normal logs.

docs.title: Machine-interface parity
docs.text:
CLI, machine JSON and MCP MUST expose the same credential classification and MUST NOT conflate classes.

Status, doctor and evidence MUST NOT claim stronger ownership, isolation or authentication guarantees than the implementation has verified.

docs.title: Versioning
docs.text:
This document defines credential/access ownership semantics version 1.

Additive evolution MAY add metadata or additional explicit classifications without weakening existing class boundaries.

A future incompatible reassignment of ownership semantics requires an explicit new contract version.

docs.title: Contract
docs.text:
Protocol identity:

baseharbor.delivery/v1

Delivery is independent from Runtime and Capability Providers.

runtime != capability != delivery

docs.title: direct
docs.text:
BaseHarbor owns reconciliation.

  • owner: baseharbor
  • provider: direct

docs.title: delegated
docs.text:
An external reconciler owns reconciliation.

  • owner: external
  • provider: implementation identifier such as a future Argo CD or Flux provider

Exactly one reconciliation owner is valid for a managed resource set.

docs.title: Placement
docs.text:
Where applicable Delivery uses the same placement vocabulary as other provider axes:

  • application
  • shared
  • external

docs.title: Hard invariants
docs.text:
• Delivery Provider products never enter portable Application capability intent.
  • Runtime Provider does not decide direct/delegated ownership.
  • Capability Provider does not decide direct/delegated ownership.
  • direct and delegated ownership cannot be active simultaneously for the same managed resource set.
  • provider-native GitOps resources remain below the Delivery Provider boundary.
  • selection provenance and immutable revision may be recorded without changing portable Application Intent.

Argo CD and Flux are possible implementations, not contract semantics.

docs.title: Scope
docs.text:
This specification defines BaseHarbor authoring-time development extensions:

  • Stack Profiles;
  • Development Plans;
  • Development Adapters.

Development extensions create or validate ecosystem-native application source. They do not provision provider infrastructure and do not become runtime provider instances.

application requirement
!= development integration
!= capability provider
!= placement
!= runtime
!= delivery

docs.title: Existing standards
docs.text:
BaseHarbor reuses existing formats and ecosystem conventions instead of defining a framework:

Concern Standard / convention Schema validation JSON Schema 2020-12 Extension artifact distribution OCI Image / Distribution Go dependencies Go modules JavaScript / Next.js dependencies package.json / npm ecosystem Python dependencies pyproject.toml / Python packaging conventions Quarkus dependencies Maven / Quarkus extension conventions Telemetry OpenTelemetry / OTLP Provider connection outputs Service Binding Specification naming where applicable Portal projection Backstage Catalog Component metadata, optional and static

Devfile concepts may inform interoperability, but Devfile is not the canonical BaseHarbor Development Plan and is not a Core dependency.

docs.title: Adopted BaseHarbor contracts
docs.text:
Machine-readable authority:

  • contracts/development/v1/stack-profile.schema.json
  • contracts/development/v1/development-plan.schema.json
  • contracts/extension/v1/extension-descriptor.schema.json

docs.title: Stack Profile
docs.text:
A Stack Profile is authoring metadata.

It MUST NOT become portable application intent, deployment state, runtime state or Provider Runtime Registry state.

A profile contains stable development components and optional capability preferences. Multiple components are supported from v1.

Composition is deterministic:

  1. referenced parent profiles are resolved in declared order;
  2. identical parent values may merge;
  3. conflicting parent values fail closed;
  4. the child profile may explicitly override inherited values;
  5. cycles fail closed;
  6. the effective profile has deterministic component and capability ordering.

An implementation preference remains a preference. It MUST NOT silently become a provider/product requirement in the portable Application Contract.

docs.title: Development Plan
docs.text:
The Development Plan is an authoring-time plan and is distinct from the runtime/deployment plan.

It may contain ecosystem dependency requirements, application binding expectations, source/config actions, build conventions, health conventions and telemetry integration actions.

The plan MUST be deterministic for the same Application Contract, effective Stack Profile and adapter versions.

docs.title: Development Adapter
docs.text:
A Development Adapter MUST expose these semantics:

Descriptor
Detect
Supports
Plan
Bootstrap
Validate

An adapter MUST NOT provision capability-provider infrastructure, hide provider resolution inside application-source generation, introduce a required BaseHarbor application SDK, or require a runtime product in portable application intent.

Generated applications continue to use normal ecosystem libraries.

docs.title: Reference adapters
docs.text:
v0.4.18 defines four reference adapters:

development/go
development/nextjs
development/python
development/quarkus

The reference adapters are examples of the contract, not privileged Core semantics. A third-party adapter uses the same common extension metadata, resolution/trust rules and conformance expectations.

docs.title: Conformance
docs.text:
A conforming adapter proves: Descriptor, Detection, Contract mapping, Development planning, Bootstrap, Binding portability, Capability integration, Inspect round-trip, Evidence validation, Idempotency, Secret safety, No provider leakage and MCP parity.

The implementation MUST converge on:

Contract
  -> Development Plan
  -> ecosystem-native implementation
  -> normal BaseHarbor inspection
  -> evidence
  -> SATISFIED

MCP parity is verified through the normal BaseHarbor machine tool baseharbor.app.new; no shell or runtime escape hatch is part of the adapter contract.

docs.title: Extension distribution and trust
docs.text:
Provider Extensions and Development Extensions share distribution mechanics, not lifecycle semantics.

Common metadata includes extension family, stable extension ID, implementation version, compatibility, platform compatibility, OCI reference, immutable digest, JSON Schema reference and signature/SBOM/attestation references.

Resolution is fail-closed when multiple candidates are ambiguous. Trust policy may require digest, signature, SBOM and/or attestation metadata before an extension is accepted.

Tags are discovery aliases. Immutable digest is authoritative identity when artifact distribution is used.

docs.title: Backstage boundary
docs.text:
Backstage support is an emitted-contract integration, not a Development Adapter family and not a Core dependency.

catalog-info.yaml emission is optional. Portal owner is explicit and portal lifecycle is never derived from BaseHarbor environment. Runtime, target, provider placement and credentials MUST NOT leak into emitted Catalog metadata.

See ADR 0016 and docs/how-to/backstage.md.

docs.title: Compatibility impact
docs.text:
These contracts add authoring metadata only.

They do not change existing portable Application Contract semantics, capability-provider placement semantics or runtime-provider semantics. Brownfield baha app init and greenfield baha app new converge on the same Application Contract and repository inspection/evidence model.

docs.title: Extension Artifact Trust v1
docs.text:
Status: implementation candidate for v0.4.22 (#771); not the v0.5 contract freeze.

The descriptor baseharbor.extension/v1 describes extension identity, implementation version, an OCI reference, an immutable SHA-256 digest and public publisher/signature/SBOM/attestation references. It applies independently to capability, runtime, delivery, development, workload-source and Target Access extensions; their behavioral contracts remain separate.

docs.title: Verification and policy
docs.text:
baseharbor.extension-trust/v1 reports two independent results:

Verification Meaning verified The configured backend verified the selected immutable artifact. Individual evidence types have separate verified flags. unverifiable No usable verifier, no immutable digest or an unavailable verification backend. invalid Invalid metadata, an invalid proof, digest mismatch or a contradictory publisher claim. Policy decision Meaning trusted The artifact satisfies the effective operator/deployment policy. denied Policy requirements are not satisfied; a typed code and next action explain why.

A policy can allow an unverified local artifact explicitly by requiring no verification. This never changes its verification status to verified. Invalid verification always denies, including under permissive policy. Requiring a signature, SBOM or attestation requires verified evidence, not only a reference. A publisher allow-list compares the identity supplied by the verification backend, not an unverified descriptor claim.

Example: a backend verifies digest D and publisher acme, including the signature. A production policy allowing only publisher other returns publisher_denied despite the valid signature.

docs.title: Verification backend boundary
docs.text:
extension.Verifier is configured by the operator and verifies artifact bytes and evidence against the selected digest. It is not selected by untrusted descriptor data. There is no required signing vendor, registry or hosted service. Absence of a backend fails closed when verification is required; the implementation does not simulate cryptographic verification from metadata.

The result is normalized to canonical public fields. Raw backend error text is not returned because it can contain registry credentials. Public references must not contain URL credentials or query parameters. Digest-qualified OCI references must agree with the separately declared digest.

Trust policy stays outside portable Application Intent. Artifact resolution returns a structured verification and policy decision even when denied. Errors distinguish unverifiable evidence, invalid verification, missing required metadata and publisher-policy denial.

docs.title: Machine-readable contract
docs.text: The authoritative schemas are contracts/extension/v1/extension-descriptor.schema.json and contracts/extension/v1/extension-trust.schema.json in the source repository. These trust semantics are independent from provider behavioral conformance.

docs.title: Concrete standards backend
docs.text:
The operator-configured JWSVerifier recomputes SHA-256 from bounded OCI manifest bytes fetched by ArtifactReader at the selected digest. It verifies RFC 7515 asymmetric JWS evidence over in-toto v1 Statements with artifact subjects bound to that digest. The reference implementation accepts EdDSA, ES256, RS256 and PS256; key IDs resolve only to operator-configured public keys and publisher identities. Embedded keys and key URLs do not establish trust.

SBOM statements use SPDX or CycloneDX predicate identities; provenance statements use SLSA Provenance v1. Verified flags mean authenticated, digest-bound evidence, not a claim of an achieved SLSA level or a vulnerability-free artifact. Declared evidence that is unavailable yields unverifiable; invalid signatures, wrong subjects or modified manifests yield invalid. A valid publisher signature can still be denied by deployment policy.

OCI/evidence transport remains operator-configured and separate from the verifier. This backend is one supported implementation behind the common interface, without requiring a signing vendor or replacing any family's behavioral contract.

Standards: JWS RFC 7515 and in-toto Statement v1.

docs.title: Declarative input resolution
docs.text:
v0.4 introduces a reusable input resolver so CLI prompts are a presentation layer rather than the source of application/deployment question logic.

The resolver lives in internal/applicationinput and models four concerns independently:

  • default values: safe values BaseHarbor can choose without operator interaction;
  • generated values: values produced through an explicit generator callback;
  • external values: values that must come from protected state, explicit automation input or a user/operator;
  • conditional values: inputs that become required only when another resolved value selects a matching path.

Every definition can also be marked Secret. Secret values remain available to the caller for delivery to a secret/capability provider, but PersistableValues deliberately excludes them and Value.String() renders them as <redacted>.

docs.title: Resolution order
docs.text:
For each declared input BaseHarbor resolves, in order:

  1. an explicitly supplied value;
  2. the declared safe default;
  3. a generated value, when generation is declared and required;
  4. otherwise an unresolved requirement when the input is required or its required-if condition matches.

The resolver itself never reads stdin, writes files, selects a provider or logs values. That makes the same model reusable by CLI/TUI, API, future GUI, agents and CI.

docs.title: v0.4 CLI reference integration
docs.text:
Repository deployment initialization uses the resolver for:

  • hostname
  • tls_mode
  • cert_dir, required only when tls_mode=existing

Interactive baha app init asks only for unresolved values. Existing protected deployment state and explicitly supplied flags are treated as already resolved.

Automation can inject declared non-secret deployment values explicitly:

baha app init --yes \
  --input hostname=mail.example.com \
  --input tls_mode=existing \
  --input cert_dir=/secure/certificates

The existing dedicated flags remain compatible:

baha app init --yes \
  --hostname mail.example.com \
  --tls existing \
  --cert-dir /secure/certificates

Conflicting values supplied through both mechanisms fail instead of silently choosing one.

baha up uses the same declarations. When the repository contract and protected deployment state already satisfy every required input, it asks no questions. If values are missing in an interactive terminal, only those unresolved values are requested. Non-interactive mode uses only defined safe defaults/derivations and never invents an external certificate path.

docs.title: TLS reference cases
docs.text:
• Local/non-public deployment: tls_mode=local is a safe default when public TLS is not required.
  • Public TLS with a known non-local hostname: non-interactive safe resolution may select acme; issuance remains a provider capability outside the resolver.
  • Existing/BYOC certificate: choosing existing makes cert_dir conditionally required; the existing certificate detection, key matching, SAN/FQDN validation and normalized protected storage continue to run after resolution.

The resolver therefore decides which inputs are needed, while the TLS implementation continues to validate and apply the selected mode.

docs.title: Boundary with the portable application contract
docs.text: An application may eventually declare generic required inputs in the portable contract. Runtime/provider products, secret values and operator security policy do not belong there. The resolver consumes declarations and supplied context; provider selection and secret storage remain separate concerns.

docs.title: Scope
docs.text:
This specification defines the authenticated HTTPS projection of the BaseHarbor Machine Interface used by Console and other web-capable machine clients.

The public envelope schema is contracts/machine/v1/control.schema.json. Its discovery, execute_request, execution, event and error_result definitions describe the serialized Core records. control.golden.json contains explicitly synthetic examples generated from Core's types and registries by go run ./scripts/tools/machine-control-fixtures. Consumers pin both files to an immutable public Core commit and retain their SHA-256 digests. Envelope validation does not replace operation-specific input validation, authentication or policy.

The HTTP interface is a transport over the same BaseHarbor semantic operations used by CLI, JSON and MCP. It MUST NOT introduce a second lifecycle, desired-state store, authorization model or runtime abstraction.

docs.title: Security boundary
docs.text:
All machine HTTP endpoints:

  • MUST be served only by the BaseHarbor TLS management listener;
  • MUST reject plaintext HTTP with no downgrade fallback;
  • MUST pass through the existing authenticated operator HTTP middleware;
  • MUST bind the verified transport principal into the shared Machine Operator Authorization boundary;
  • MUST preserve operation safety, policy and confirmation semantics;
  • MUST keep ordinary responses, execution metadata and event metadata secret-safe.

Browser clients use memory-only bearer authentication against the configured same-origin HTTPS Core endpoint. Origin-bearing requests from a different authority are rejected; Core does not authenticate browser cookies. Console transports must reject foreign discovered destinations and redirects before forwarding a credential. SSE therefore uses authenticated fetch streaming, not a cookie-only EventSource assumption.

Each admitted event/log/exec stream ends at the earlier of verified token expiry and five minutes. Provider streams close on request cancellation/deadline; socket writes are bounded to 30 seconds, clamped to the session deadline. Reconnection requires authentication and authorization again. This does not promise instant revocation of identity-provider group changes within an issued token's lifetime.

Transport authentication and operator authorization are separate requirements. A valid TLS connection does not by itself authorize an operation.

docs.title: Console installation topology
docs.text:
The default is one optional Console connected directly to one selected Core in one BaseHarbor installation and security boundary. Serve Console and protected Core HTTP on the same HTTPS origin. Core remains the authority for lifecycle, policy, identities and secrets. The Console owns no parallel authority or installation state. Core checks browser Origin against the destination HTTPS authority, including its port; forwarding headers cannot authorize a foreign Origin, and duplicate Origin headers are rejected.

The v0.4.23 Console rejects a configured foreign Core before authentication and pins all discovered destinations to the selected Core. It does not provide a central multi-Core backend, Dev-to-Prod forwarding or installation federation. Cross-origin operation requires a separate explicit trusted-origin design; it is not enabled by CORS headers or redirects in this release. A future client-side installation selector must authenticate directly to each newly selected Core and discard the previous installation's credentials and streams.

docs.title: Discovery
docs.text:
GET /api/v1/machine/discovery

Returns the current machine contract, execution contract, semantic operations and negotiated HTTP capabilities.

Clients MUST discover operations rather than infer support from CLI spelling.

HTTP discovery lists only the operations implemented by the selected HTTP executor. It takes their descriptors and safety metadata from the shared Core registry. The same support registry selects execution handlers and rejects unimplemented operations before creating an execution. A semantic operation available through another projection does not imply HTTP support.

HTTP discovery also returns an http map of named endpoint bindings, each with href, method and optional protocol. The same Core registry installs the routes and produces these descriptors. Browsers bootstrap only the documented discovery endpoint, then use these bindings for execution and streams. Named {execution_id} and {stream_id} placeholders accept validated resource IDs. Every resolved destination remains pinned to the configured HTTPS Core origin; discovery never authorizes a redirect, credential-bearing URL or foreign origin.

docs.title: Executions
docs.text:
POST /api/v1/machine/executions

Request:

{
  "operation_id": "status",
  "context": {
    "application": "demo",
    "environment": "prod",
    "target": "prod-eu"
  },
  "input": {}
}

context.environment is mandatory. Context selectors are the authorization scope. Operation input MUST NOT override an explicitly authorized application, environment, target, workspace or runtime resource.

Accepted operations return HTTP 202 with an Execution v1 resource and a Location header.

The execution model exposes:

  • stable execution_id;
  • semantic operation_id;
  • stable actor reference;
  • bounded operation context;
  • pending | running | succeeded | failed | cancelled;
  • structured progress;
  • structured result or typed error;
  • start/finish timestamps.

Typed errors may include an object-shaped details field in the error response, execution and event. Provider-change failures expose the current redacted impact plan through this field, using the versioned provider-impact contract. Consumers must preserve the failed state and display the consequences. Details do not grant approval; any retry still requires the current plan-bound acknowledgements and separate explicit consent for data deletion.

Operation input is not retained in ordinary execution metadata. The semantic executor rejects unknown fields, duplicate keys at every depth, non-object input, invalid UTF-8, nesting beyond 64 levels and trailing JSON values without including submitted field names or values in its validation failure.

docs.title: Execution status and events
docs.text:
GET /api/v1/machine/executions/{execution_id}

Returns the structured execution resource.

GET /api/v1/machine/executions/{execution_id}/events

Returns semantic Server-Sent Events using the Machine Event v1 envelope.

Admission headers are flushed immediately. Every 15 seconds the stream may emit an SSE comment (: keepalive) to preserve idle HTTPS transport during a long provider operation. Comments are not Machine Events: they have no sequence, progress or result and MUST NOT trigger application continuation. They neither extend the five-minute/token-expiry observation deadline nor replay execution.

The initial event vocabulary includes:

  • operation.started;
  • operation.progress;
  • operation.succeeded;
  • operation.failed;
  • operation.cancelled;
  • application/provider/target/runtime-resource state events for compatible future producers.

Execution metadata and event streams are bound to the authenticated execution actor. One authenticated operator MUST NOT read another operator's execution stream merely by knowing the execution identifier.

docs.title: Navigation operations
docs.text:
The semantic machine registry includes structured navigation operations required by Console.
